tools.name: create_image_pro_flash
tools.description:
Create one Pro Flash pixel-art image with an optional left-box style image.

Custom sizes (Beta) accept width and height from 16 to 256 in multiples of 4 pixels.
Query get_pro_flash_capabilities for native presets.
The style image accepts {url}, {base64}, or {source_image_id}; prefer URLs
for uploaded images. Style art must fit the native canvas without resizing.
For several assets of one game, pass the same anchor sprite as style_image on
every call (e.g. the hero's south rotation URL from get_character); without it
each call picks its own look.
style_options selects color_palette, outline, detail and shading independently.
Default style uses existing PixelLab art. For a console or palette look (1-bit,
Game Boy, PICO-8, any palette from Lospec) pass `palette` as its hex colours plus
`palette_name`: the image is drawn for the palette and every pixel of the result
is one of its colours; the style image keeps lending its look. Returns one image.
Failed pixel grids use image-to-pixel-art with fixer on the generated box.
Poll get_image(job_id); use source_image_id after completion.

Cost: by LONGEST SIDE — 5 generations up to 96px, 6 from 100 to 208, 9 from
212 to 256, for one image. A non-square canvas goes by its longer side, so
128x72 is 6 and 32x96 is 5. This is the whole Pro Flash ladder (create, edit
and inpaint charge the same), and it is NOT the Pro tools' 10/15/25 tier.
No parameter caps a charge, and the quote is labelled provisional rather
than a contractual cap — but the ladder above is what actually gets billed,
so treat those figures as the price.
get_pro_flash_capabilities(operation=, width=, height=) prices an exact size
for free before you spend.

width.description: Native sizes: 16x16 (experimental), 24x24, 32x32, 32x48, 48x48, 64x64, 96x64, 96x96, 128x128. Custom size (Beta): integer width 16–256 and height 16–256. Both dimensions must be multiples of 4 pixels. Pixel-grid recovery uses image-to-pixel-art with fixer when needed. No native image resizing.

style_image.description: Style anchor. Exactly ONE of its three sources: `url` also accepts an `upload:<id>` from get_upload_url or a data: URL, and `source_image_id` is an image you own (what a Pro Flash job returns). It must fit INSIDE the output canvas both ways — a larger one is refused, so crop it; resizing pixel art is never the answer. Reuse one anchor across calls to keep a set consistent.

usage_description.description: How this reference should guide appearance.

style_options.description: Choose which visual traits to copy from the style image.

palette.description: Target palette, 2 to 256 hex colours as a JSON array, e.g. ["#081820", "#346856", "#88c070", "#e0f8d0"] for Game Boy or ["#000000", "#ffffff"] for 1-bit. The image is drawn for these colours and every pixel of the result is one of them.

palette_name.description: Optional name of the palette (e.g. 'Game Boy', 'PICO-8'); naming it helps the look.

max_colors.description: At most this many colours in the image (2-64). With a palette, they are picked from it.

tools.name: edit_image_pro_flash
tools.description:
Edit one Pro Flash image at its unchanged native canvas size.

Supply image_url (preferred), image_base64, or an owned source_image_id.
method=text requires description; method=reference requires reference_image
({url}, {base64}, or {source_image_id}). References must fit the source canvas.
No-background defaults to the source's transparency. Optional palette
correction matches source colors. Query get_pro_flash_capabilities for exact
shapes. Returns one queued image; poll get_image(job_id), then download.

Cost: by the SOURCE canvas's longest side — 5 generations up to 96px, 6 from
100 to 208, 9 from 212 to 256, for one image. The same ladder as Pro Flash
create and inpaint, and cheaper than edit_image's 10/15/25 tier at every
size. get_pro_flash_capabilities(operation="edit", width=, height=) prices
an exact size for free.

reference_image.description: Exactly ONE of its three sources (`url` also accepts an `upload:<id>` from get_upload_url or a data: URL). Required when method='reference'. It must fit the edit canvas, which is the source image's own size because Pro Flash never rescales — crop it instead.

usage_description.description: How this reference should guide appearance.

no_background.description: Background removal on the result. Left out it follows the source: on if the source has any non-opaque pixel, off if it is fully opaque. Off, the edit is drawn on a plain white background, so a transparent sprite sent with false comes back flattened onto white.

use_color_palette_correction.description: Hold the edit to the SOURCE image's own colours: the prompt asks for them and every visible output pixel is then mapped to the nearest colour already in the source, so the edit introduces no new colour. Use it for a locked palette or a repair that must not recolour; leave it off when the edit needs a colour the source does not have (a red cape on a grey knight). Needs a source with visible pixels. Neither this tool nor inpaint_image_pro_flash takes a palette LIST - create_image_pro and image_to_pixelart_pro_flash are the Pro Flash tools that do.

tools.name: inpaint_image
tools.description:
Regenerate one region of an image, keeping everything else pixel-identical.

This is the repair tool: fix a malformed hand, erase a stray pixel cluster,
swap just the cape, add an item to a specific spot. The area outside the
mask is frozen, so the rest of the sprite cannot drift.

Give the area as a rectangle (easiest — you only need coordinates):
  inpaint_image(image_base64=<png>, description="a clean open hand",
                mask_x=18, mask_y=30, mask_width=14, mask_height=14)
or supply your own mask (white = regenerate, black = keep):
  inpaint_image(image_base64=<png>, description="...", mask_image_base64=<png>)

Related: edit_image rewrites the WHOLE image from an instruction (no mask);
create_map_object generates a new object matching a background's style and
returns a transparent cutout, not your edited image.

Image must be 32x32-512x512; above 256px on a side needs a Tier 2 plan.
Cost: 10 generations for any SQUARE canvas up to 256x256 (so 64x64 and 88x88
are both 10), 15 up to 341x341, 25 above. The whole image sets the price, not
the mask. A NON-SQUARE canvas is measured against the nearest of ten aspect
ratios, so BOTH sides count and neither the longest side nor the area decides
it. The 10 ceiling then the 15 ceiling, by ratio: 1:1 256x256 then 341x341 |
5:4 288x232 then 384x309 | 4:3 300x224 then 400x298 | 3:2 316x212 then
421x282 | 16:9 344x192 then 458x256 | 21:9 396x168 then 528x224 (that last
one is past this tool's own 512px side limit, so it is unreachable); a portrait
canvas takes its own ratio's pair swapped (4:5, 3:4, 2:3, 9:16, and anything
taller than 9:16 snaps to 9:16). A canvas fitting inside a ceiling costs that
band and anything past the second one is 25, so 360x168 is 10 and 168x360 is
15, and 220x256 is 10 where 220x400 is 15 and 220x512 is 25.
Generation time: ~30-90 seconds (async).
Poll with get_image(job_id).

description.description: What should appear in the masked area (e.g. 'a clean four-finger hand holding a sword', 'plain grass, no object').

image_base64.description: Base64 PNG to repair. 32x32 to 512x512. Everything outside the mask is preserved exactly. PREFER image_url — MCP clients routinely truncate large inline base64, which corrupts the image.

image_url.description: Alternative to image_base64: an https, data: or `upload:<id>` URL to the PNG to repair. PREFER THIS for anything but a tiny sprite — inline base64 is often cut off mid-string by MCP clients. Give one, not both.

mask_x.description: Left edge of the rectangular area to regenerate.

mask_y.description: Top edge of the rectangular area to regenerate.

mask_width.description: Width of the area to regenerate.

mask_height.description: Height of the area to regenerate.

mask_image_base64.description: Custom mask, same size as the image: WHITE = regenerate, BLACK = keep. Use instead of mask_x/y/width/height when the area isn't a rectangle. A greyscale (mode L) PNG is accepted and converted, but keep it pure 0/255 — white and black are the only values with a defined meaning. The size must match exactly; masks are never rescaled.

mask_image_url.description: Alternative to mask_image_base64: an https, data: or `upload:<id>` URL to the mask PNG. Give one, not both.

crop_to_mask.description: Confine generated content to the mask boundary for clean edges.

no_background.description: Background handling. Default (unset) follows the input: a sprite with transparency stays transparent, an opaque image stays opaque. Pass False to flatten a transparent input onto white.

project_id.description: Internal Game Builder project context; the finished image is linked after generation.

tools.name: inpaint_image_pro_flash
tools.description:
Replace white-mask pixels with Pro Flash, preserving unmasked RGBA bytes exactly.

Source: image_url, image_base64, or owned source_image_id. Mask: a rectangle
(all four mask_x/y/width/height), OR a same-size mask PNG via base64/URL.
Mask RGB must be pure white=generate or black=keep; mask alpha is ignored.
Empty masks are rejected. crop_to_mask is always true. Changes-only output
is transparent outside the mask; Modify current layer returns a composite.
Optional context_image requires bounding_box locating the source and is at
most three times its native dimensions. No images or masks are rescaled.
Query get_pro_flash_capabilities for shapes; poll the job with get_image.

Cost: by the SOURCE canvas's longest side, not the mask — 5 generations up to
96px, 6 from 100 to 208, 9 from 212 to 256, for one image. So a 64x64 repair
is 5 and 128x64 is 6, against inpaint_image's 10 for either. Shrinking the
mask does not lower it. get_pro_flash_capabilities(operation="inpaint",
width=, height=) prices an exact size for free.

mask_image_base64.description: Mask PNG, exactly the source size. EVERY pixel's RGB must be pure white (generate) or pure black (keep): a grey or coloured pixel is refused, so remove any antialiasing, and a mask with no white at all is refused too. The mask's own alpha is ignored. Unlike inpaint_image, which does not check this, Pro Flash enforces it. Or give the four mask_x/y/width/height instead.

mask_image_url.description: Same mask as mask_image_base64, from an https, data: or `upload:<id>` URL.

context_image.description: The surrounding scene to match, not a style reference. Pass it WITH bounding_box or not at all. At most 3x the source canvas in each dimension and never rescaled. Exactly ONE of its three sources.

usage_description.description: How this reference should guide appearance.

bounding_box.description: Where the source canvas sits inside context_image: width/height must equal the source size, and the box must lie entirely within the context image.

no_background.description: Background removal on the GENERATED pixels. Left out it follows the source: on if the source has any non-opaque pixel, off if it is fully opaque. Removal runs before the frozen pixels are copied back, so masked pixels CAN come back transparent (how a bigger hairstyle keeps gaps around it) and pixels outside the mask are untouched either way. Off, the render is drawn on a background, so the masked area comes back opaque.

output_method.description: What comes back, always at the source's own size. `Modify current layer` (default) is the whole sprite with the mask area replaced. `Modify current layer, only changes` and `New layer with changes` are that same canvas holding ONLY the masked pixels, fully transparent everywhere else - a layer to drop over your own art. Every pixel outside the mask is copied from your source byte for byte, and that copy is the LAST step, after background removal and palette work, so nothing outside the mask can shift.

Create a Pro Flash character from text, including its first image and eight V3 views.

Supply description, optional width/height (default 64x64), and style_image.
For a cast that matches (enemies drawn like the hero), pass the same anchor
sprite as style_image on every call (e.g. the hero's south rotation URL from
get_character); without it each call picks its own look.
Animals: set template_id (bear, cat, dog, horse, lion) and keep 64x64 or larger
(at 48x48 a cat came out small). Say "standing on all four legs" if it will
walk: a cat and a dog came out sitting without it.
Custom sizes (Beta) accept width and height from 16 to 256 in multiples of 4 pixels.
First-direction generation is built in; no separate preview tool is needed.
Alternatively reuse source_image_id or first_frame_url/base64 and omit size
and style settings. A chosen image is preserved with transparent V3 padding,
and only rotations are charged. Never provide both image sources.
Poll get_character(character_id) or the returned outer background job until
completed, including skeleton preparation, before downloading or animating.

charges. The image goes by longest side — 5 generations up to 96px, 6 from

tools.name: add_to_project
tools.description:
Let a game project use a character, object, tileset, map, room or UI asset you
already own, or file an asset (gallery images, tile groups and isometric tiles
too) into a game or folder on the website.
Songs and sound effects go in a game too: the game gets their audio file.

A game gets the asset in its asset library; one not yet in any folder is
also filed under that game. A folder only groups assets on the website: the
asset moves into it and keeps every game it is in. Characters and objects
move with all their states, a UI asset with its elements. Tile groups and
isometric tiles have no asset library to join: they are filed under the
project you name (a tile group reaches a game as a map's tile layer).

A project's game can only load art that belongs to that project, and until
now the only way to put art there was to create it from inside Game Builder.
Art made anywhere else — this MCP server, the website — was invisible to
every game, so the only route was to generate it a second time and pay for
it again.

A saved VFX effect id (My effects, vfx_workbench export) is not linked:
the reply gives its files (game pack with manifest: frame order, timing,
anchor) as download links and the command that puts them in the game.

The kind is worked out from the id; you do not have to say which it is.
Calling twice is harmless.

project_id.description: A game or folder project, from list_projects

asset_id.description: A character, object, tileset, map, room, UI asset, Tiles Pro tile group, isometric tile or gallery image you own — the id from list_characters, list_objects, list_topdown_tilesets, list_maps, list_rooms, list_ui_assets, list_tiles_pro, list_isometric_tiles or list_images —, a song_id or sound_effect_id (list_music, list_sound_effects) or audio file id, or a saved VFX effect id (My effects)

tools.name: remove_from_project
tools.description:
Stop a game project from using a character, object, tileset, map, room, UI
asset, song or sound effect, or take an asset out of a folder (or a tile group
or isometric tile out of the game it is filed under).

This unlinks the art from the project. It does NOT delete the art: the
asset stays in your library and can be added back at any time, and any
other project using it is untouched. Use delete_character / delete_object /
delete_topdown_tileset / delete_map / delete_room to actually destroy something.

Until now add_to_project had no inverse, so a project could accumulate art
it no longer used — and a map that fails to export blocks every deploy of
that project, with no way back out.

The kind is worked out from the id; you do not have to say which it is.
Calling twice is harmless.

project_id.description: The game project or folder, from list_projects

asset_id.description: A character, object, tileset, map, room, UI asset, tile group, isometric tile, image, song, sound effect or audio file currently in the project — the id you passed to add_to_project

tools.name: manage_project
tools.description:
Manage your projects (list_projects shows them). A folder only groups your assets on
the website: no workspace, git repo or deploy; file assets into it with
add_to_project. Renaming keeps a game's address. Deleting a folder keeps its assets
(they go back to "No project"); game projects are deleted on the website only.
Rename and delete are for organization admins.

action.description: create_folder: make a folder (needs name). rename: rename a game project or folder (needs project_id and name). delete_folder: delete a folder (needs project_id); its assets are kept.

project_id.description: For rename / delete_folder: a project from list_projects. Leave out for create_folder.

tools.name: create_character
tools.description:
Queue a character with 4 or 8 directions. Returns its id at once; poll
get_character (~2-5 min).

Modes (default v3):
- v3: the most detailed sprites, 8 directions, up to 256px, drawn from the
  description as written. Humanoid only without a reference.
- v3 + reference image is the default way to turn a sprite you have into a
  character (not create_8_direction_object): kept as drawn as the south view,
  so it must face the viewer straight on. Humanoids and quadrupeds;
  direction_images adds directions you drew.
- pro: 8 directions, max 128px. To match an existing character
  (style_character_id) or a style picture, design from concept art, or rotate a
  sprite facing any way or a body v3 gets wrong (Pro rotate). The only mode
  taking palette and max_colors.
- standard: the cheapest, 4 or 8 directions, max 128px.

A quadruped from text: create_character_pro_flash(template_id=...) at 64px, or
mode="pro" or "standard" here with body_type="quadruped". No seed; for one look
across characters use style_character_id or a reference image.

Cost: standard 1 generation at ANY size. v3 from text by size: 2 for 16-90, 3
for 91-128, 4 for 129-156, 5 for 157-181, 6 for 182-202, 7 for 203-221, 8 for
222-239, 9 for 240-256; with a reference, ceil(w*h*8/65536) of its own
size, minimum 1 (64x64 = 1, 128x128 = 2); every direction yours is an import,
0.25. pro 10 up to 85px, 15 for 86-113, 25 for 114-128, which is also its size
cap.

Full reference (all rules, sizes and prices): search_help(tool="create_character").

description.description: Character appearance, e.g. 'cute wizard with blue robes'. v3 without a reference draws a two-armed, two-legged figure whatever this says; for an animal see body_type.

body_type.description: "quadruped" (4-legged animals) needs template. Quadrupeds work in mode="standard", mode="pro", and mode="v3" WITH a reference image; v3 without a reference image is humanoid only.

template.description: Required with body_type='quadruped': `bear`, `cat`, `dog`, `horse`, `lion`. Ignored for humanoids.

mode.description: Default "v3". See the tool description for when to pick each.

n_directions.description: Ignored in pro and in v3 without a reference (always 8). With a v3 reference, 4 keeps south/east/north/west.

reference_image_base64.description: reference_image_url as PNG base64 (max 256x256): for v3 it must face straight-on, toward the viewer. Prefer the URL above ~32x32: clients truncate long base64.

style_character_id.description: pro only: id of your completed 8-direction character whose style the new one copies; its drawn part (not its canvas) must fit size, and an unset size follows it. Not with a reference image.

style_image_url.description: pro only: a pixel-art picture whose style the new character copies (https, upload:<id> or data: URL); its visible part must fit size, max 128. Not with a reference image.

reference_image_url.description: https, data: or `upload:<id>` URL of the sprite to rotate (v3 or pro, max 256x256). v3 takes it as south: it must face STRAIGHT-ON, toward the viewer, or a 3/4 view offsets every direction; there is no way to declare a different facing. pro: any facing.

concept_image_url.description: pro only: concept art, a painting or a photo the character is designed from (look kept, not pose); https, data: or `upload:<id>` URL. A finished sprite to rotate goes in reference_image_url.

direction_images.description: v3 with a reference only: sprites you drew for other directions (URL, upload:<id>, data URL or PNG base64), same canvas as the reference, used as drawn; v3 draws the rest.

proportions.description: Standard, humanoids: {"type": "preset", "name": "chibi"}, presets default, chibi, cartoon, stylized, realistic_male, realistic_female, heroic; or "custom" bone sizes (format in the full reference).

size.description: Pixels, default 48 (with a reference: its own size). Max 128 in standard and pro; v3 from text takes multiples of 4. Standard stores it on a ~40% larger canvas (64 -> 92x92).

shading.description: Soft hint. Ignored in pro and v3.

text_guidance_scale.description: How closely to follow the description. Ignored in pro and v3.

view.description: Camera: "low top-down" (~20°, classic 3/4 RPG), "high top-down" (~35°), "side" (eye level), "oblique" (beta: standard, n_directions=4, max 128px).

palette.description: Target palette, 2 to 256 hex colours as a JSON array, e.g. ["#081820", "#346856", "#88c070", "#e0f8d0"] for Game Boy or ["#000000", "#ffffff"] for 1-bit. Every pixel the tool draws is one of them; pixels you supplied (a direction you drew) stay as they are.

palette_name.description: Optional name of the palette (e.g. 'Game Boy', 'PICO-8'); naming it helps the look. It only LABELS the colours you pass in palette rather than looking any up, so it cannot be sent on its own.

max_colors.description: At most this many colours (2-64). With a palette, they are picked from it. On the three tools that have a standard mode — create_character, create_topdown_tileset, animate_object — ANY palette setting needs mode='pro': standard refuses palette and max_colors, alone or together. Every other tool taking them has no standard mode and accepts them always.

tools.name: create_character_state
tools.description:
Queue a state (variant) of an existing character. The new character keeps
the source's identity, body type, and proportions, with the edit applied
consistently across all 4 or 8 rotations. Auto-waits up to 30s for the
source to complete.

A character is a group of states: `name` is the character's name (shared by
all states), and each state has its own `state_name` — defaulting to the
edit description truncated to 20 characters (a new character's first state
is named "Idle"). Pass `state_name` to name the new state explicitly.

IMPORTANT — this ALWAYS preserves the SAME individual's face and identity,
even for edits like "elderly", "wounded", or a different class/role. It makes
a variant OF this character (different outfit/pose/state), NOT a new character.
To make a DIFFERENT character in the same art style, use create_character with
matching size/view/outline/shading/detail params (and a v3 reference image if
you want to match the look) — not create_character_state.

Returns a new character_id grouped with the source via group_id. Inspect
sibling states with `get_character` on either id.

`palette` (hex colours, plus `palette_name`) puts every direction of the state on
those colours, the source's rotations first; it can't be combined with
use_color_palette_from_reference (max_colors alone can).

Cost: ONE charge for the whole state — every rotation the source has, 4 or 8,
is redrawn and billed together, so there is no per-direction price and an
8-direction character costs the same as a 4-direction one. It is 10, 15 or 25
generations, set by the size of the character's own ART rather than its
canvas. The rotations' content is squared, padded 20% and
floored at 32px; that cell costs 10 up to 84px, 15 from 85 to 112, 25 above.
The art cannot be bigger than the frame, so a character whose frames are
70px or smaller ALWAYS costs 10 (a 48x48 character is 10), and one up to
93px never costs more than 15. Setting override_width/override_height is the
exception: an enlarged state is priced on the NEW frame size directly, art
or no art, against the same 84/112 thresholds — so enlarging a 48x48
character to 128x128 turns a 10 into a 25. Only above that is the charge genuinely
unknown before the call, because it depends on how much of the frame the art
fills; the balance check reserves only the 10 floor, so a call there CAN
charge more than it reserved — leave 25 of headroom or check get_balance.

Generation time: ~1-5 minutes (async). Poll with get_character(character_id).

character_id.description: Source character UUID to create a state of

edit_description.description: Edit instructions describing the new state (e.g. 'sitting down', 'wearing red armor', 'fighting pose').

state_name.description: Name for the new state (e.g. 'Sitting', 'Red Armor'). Defaults to the edit description truncated to 20 characters.

use_color_palette_from_reference.description: Snap the edited rotations to the source character's existing color palette so the new state stays color-consistent with the original. Do not enable when the edit is meant to introduce new colors.

override_width.description: Optional larger canvas WIDTH for the state — reach for it when the edit adds something big (a weapon, wings) needing room beyond the character's tight canvas. Multiple of 4, no smaller than the source width. Pair with override_height; omit both to keep the source size.

override_height.description: Optional larger canvas HEIGHT for the state (see override_width). Multiple of 4, no smaller than the source height.

palette.description: Target palette, 2 to 256 hex colours as a JSON array, e.g. ["#081820", "#346856", "#88c070", "#e0f8d0"] for Game Boy or ["#000000", "#ffffff"] for 1-bit. Every pixel the tool draws is one of them; pixels you supplied (a direction you drew) stay as they are.

palette_name.description: Optional name of the palette (e.g. 'Game Boy', 'PICO-8'); naming it helps the look. It only LABELS the colours you pass in palette rather than looking any up, so it cannot be sent on its own.

max_colors.description: At most this many colours (2-64). With a palette, they are picked from it. On the three tools that have a standard mode — create_character, create_topdown_tileset, animate_object — ANY palette setting needs mode='pro': standard refuses palette and max_colors, alone or together. Every other tool taking them has no standard mode and accepts them always.

tools.name: animate_character
tools.description:
Queue an animation for a character. Returns job ids at once; ~2-4 min.

Modes (from what you pass; override with `mode`):
- template: template_animation_id, a clip such as walking or breathing-idle.
- v3 (default without a template id): your motion in action_description.
- pixminimax (beta): action_description, clips up to 40 frames, cheap at large sizes.
- skeleton-v3 (beta): a template clip on the character's own skeleton (still
  redrawn each frame, colours hold closer), or without template_animation_id a
  motion you write as poses (the first call returns the format, free).
- template_action: the website's walk/run/sprint/idle and strike animations.

Template and skeleton-v3 animate all the character's directions; v3 and
pixminimax animate south unless you pass directions. To add directions to an
animation, pass its animation_group_id and animation_name. A poor result: delete
it, retry, or try the next mode (template, v3, pixminimax).

Cost: template 1 generation per direction up to ~92px (more above; the receipt
gives the ceiling). v3 ceil(w*h*frames/65536) per direction on the generated
canvas (64px at 8 frames = 1, 96-128px = 2-3). pixminimax 1-6 per direction by
size and frames. skeleton-v3 2-4 per direction.

Full reference (every option, prices by size, all clip ids):
search_help(tool="animate_character").

template_animation_id.description: A template clip (template and skeleton-v3 modes), e.g. walking, breathing-idle, taking-punch. get_character lists the character's available_animations; an unknown id is refused, free, with the full list. No hurt/dash/cast clips: use taking-punch, running-slide, fireball. Omit for a custom motion in action_description.

action_description.description: The movement or pose only, e.g. 'walking stealthily', 'casting spell'; no locations or objects. Defaults from template_animation_id.

animation_name.description: Stored as display_name. Appending to an animation_group_id: repeat the group's name, it is not inherited.

animation_group_id.description: Add these directions to an existing animation (the [group: ...] id from get_character) instead of starting a new one, e.g. the missing directions of a partial run. Pass animation_name too.

directions.description: e.g. ['south', 'east'] (south, north, east, west, south-east, south-west, north-east, north-west). Default: all the character's directions in template mode, south in custom modes.

ai_freedom.description: Template mode only: how far poses may leave the template (0 = rigid).

mode.description: Inferred when left out: template with template_animation_id, else v3. See the tool description.

frame_count.description: v3: 4-16, even, width x height x frames <= 8 x 256 x 256. pixminimax: a multiple of 4, 4-40. Custom skeleton-v3: 3-15. Template clips keep their own count.

custom_start_frame_base64.description: v3/pixminimax, ONE direction (ask the user which if unsaid): a start pose instead of the character's rotation, max 256x256.

end_frame_base64.description: v3/pixminimax, ONE direction: a pose to animate toward, same size as the start. A target the last frame is drawn toward, not a stored frame.

custom_start_frame_url.description: https, data: or `upload:<id>` URL instead of custom_start_frame_base64; prefer it for large images (clients truncate long base64).

end_frame_url.description: https, data: or `upload:<id>` URL instead of end_frame_base64.

keep_first_frame.description: v3/pixminimax: keep the start frame as frame 0 (frame_count + 1 stored); false stores exactly frame_count.

subject_description.description: pixminimax only: what the character is, one noun phrase. Read from the image if left out; fill it in if a job is declined.

initial_pose.description: pixminimax only: the first frame's pose. Read from the image if left out.

poses.description: Custom skeleton-v3 (no template_animation_id): one pose object per frame. Call first without poses or move for the format and this character's numbers (free).

scale.description: Custom skeleton-v3 with poses: one size per frame (1 = rest size).

move.description: Custom skeleton-v3: a library move instead of writing every pose, e.g. {"name": "run", "energy": 1.2}, or a list of moves with "frames": [first, last]. The free first call lists the moves.

template_action.description: A website template animation (gaits, idle, strikes) on pixminimax (default) or v3, written for each direction; leave action_description and template_animation_id out. Its own frame count; priced like a custom animation of that length.

motion_adjustments.description: skeleton-v3 with template_animation_id: the website's motion sliders, 1 = the template's own motion, e.g. {"stride": 1.25}. Four-legged characters: stride and posture only.

arm_swing.description: How far the arms swing around their average pose: 0 holds them still, 1 is the template's own motion, 1.5 exaggerates it. Two-legged characters only: a four-legged character's front legs follow stride.

stride.description: How far the legs swing (all four on a four-legged character): 0 holds them still, 1 is the template's own motion, 1.5 exaggerates it.

posture.description: Stands the character like the template instead of its own stance: 0 keeps its own, 1 the template's.

leg_extension.description: Straightens the legs as they reach forward and push off: 0 off, 1 full. Two-legged characters only.

direction_prompts.description: v3/pixminimax: one prompt per direction, all eight keys, the motion as seen from that side. Reused when adding directions to the group.

palette.description: 2 to 256 hex colours, e.g. ["#081820", "#88c070"]; every frame uses only these. Not in template mode.

palette_name.description: Labels the palette colours; needs palette.

max_colors.description: At most this many colours, picked from palette (needs palette).

tools.name: get_character
tools.description:
Get character details, rotation URLs, animations, and download link.
Branches by status: processing (progress+ETA), failed (error+retry), completed (full data).

Download: three ways out, and the last one needs no HTTP at all.
`/mcp/characters/{id}/download` is a ZIP of every completed state in the
group — `?states=` narrows it, taking the state IDS this tool prints on
its `state:` lines, not their names — laid out as
`<state>/rotations/<direction>.png` and
`<state>/animations/<name>/<direction>/frame_000.png` (frame_NNN, 3 digits,
from 000), plus `<state>/portrait.png` and `<state>/vocal/grid.png` where
those exist, and a top-level `metadata.json` giving each state's size,
directions, view, template_id and a `frames` map listing every file — so
the per-direction frame counts are in there as the list lengths. A frame
storage lost shows up as `MISSING_FRAMES.txt` rather than a short ZIP.
`/mcp/characters/{id}/spritesheet` is a ZIP of one sheet PNG + its layout
JSON for THIS state only: row 0 is the rotations, then one row per
animation-direction, uniform cells sized to the largest frame with the rest
transparent padding (nothing is ever resized), and the JSON gives
`cell_size`, `sheet_size`, `columns`, `pivot: "cell-center"` and a row list
naming each row's animation, `animation_group_id`, direction and
frame_count.
To get the pixels back INLINE, with no download and nothing charged:
`pixelart_workbench(argv=["inspect", "character:<id>:<direction>:<animation>"])`
returns that animation's frames as one sheet image in the tool result, with
the canvas and frame durations — `<animation>` is the display name, type or
[group: ...] id this tool prints. `join ref ref --as rows` lays several
animations out one per row (sheets hold at most 1024 px a side).

include_preview.description: Include preview image of south direction

tools.name: list_characters
tools.description:
List your characters with status. Returns compact one-line-per-character format.
Use get_character(character_id) for full details on any character.

limit.description: Maximum number of characters to return

tags.description: Comma-separated tags to filter by (ANY match). Example: 'wizard,fire'

search.description: Filter by name, case-insensitive. Matches the name shown here and the description it was created from, so 'wizard' finds 'old wizard with a staff'.

tools.name: delete_character
tools.description:
Delete ONE state of a character (the given id) with its rotations,
animations and files. Other states in the same group are untouched; the
group itself is removed only when its last state is deleted. To delete a
whole multi-state character, call this once per state id (list them with
get_character). Immediate — cannot be undone (in-flight jobs are wasted).

tools.name: update_character_tags
tools.description:
Replace ALL tags on a character (set operation, free, synchronous).

Tags organize and filter characters in list_characters. Passing an empty
list clears every tag. This replaces the full set: include existing tags
you want to keep.

character_id.description: Character UUID whose tags to replace

tags.description: Full replacement tag list (max 20 tags, 50 chars each; whitespace trimmed, case-insensitive dedup). Empty list clears all tags.

tools.name: delete_animation
tools.description:
Delete animations from a character or object. Removes storage files and database rows.
Use get_character()/get_object() first to see available animations. Omit direction to
delete all directions at once. For objects, animation_group_id (from get_object) can
be passed instead of animation_type.

animation_type.description: Animation name to delete. Characters: animation type (e.g. 'walk', 'idle', 'attack'), see get_character(). Objects: the animation name shown by get_object(). Required unless animation_group_id is provided.

direction.description: Specific direction to delete (e.g. 'south'). Omit to delete all directions of this animation.

animation_group_id.description: Animation group UUID, shown by get_character()/get_object() as [group: ...]. Selects one animation unambiguously (preferred over animation_type when a name repeats); deletes all its directions unless direction is set.

tools.name: create_map
tools.description:
Create an empty map seeded with a tileset and everything connected to it,
or with a tile group.

The map starts with no painted cells — paint it with edit_map, which grows
the bounds as you go. Tile size comes from the seed tileset. A map started
from a tile group is a tile map instead: its tiles go on tile layers with
place_map_tiles, which can stack them. A map started from a sidescroller
tileset is a sidescroller map: paint the solid ground with edit_map, and it
gets a background preset as in Map Workshop.

Being in the same family makes a terrain AVAILABLE, not blendable: only a
pair with its own tileset renders a border. Check with view_map, which names
every unpaired pair and the create_topdown_tileset call that joins it.

Cost: free, and so is every other map operation — edit_map, place_map_tiles,
place_map_object, edit_map_object, view_map, get_map — except inpaint_map,
which generates new pixels and charges for them. The rest only arrange art
you already own, so none of them touch generations or credits. What costs is
making that art first: create_topdown_tileset or create_tiles_pro for the
terrain, create_map_object for a prop.

tileset_id.description: Tileset to seed the map from (from list_topdown_tilesets). Every tileset connected to it — same tile size, sharing a base tile id — is attached too, so their terrains are available to paint. A pair still needs its OWN tileset to blend: two terrains from the family with none between them meet with a hard edge (a straight seam), and view_map names any such pair with the call that blends it. A sidescroller tileset (list_sidescroller_tilesets) makes a sidescroller map instead: each platform top is a terrain, empty cells are open air.

background.description: Sidescroller maps only: the sky behind the level, one of Map Workshop's presets. Default green_hills, the one Map Workshop gives a sidescroller map. It repeats sideways and covers the rows from y=0 down; change it in Map Workshop.

tile_group_id.description: Instead of tileset_id: a tile group (from list_tiles_pro — isometric, hex, oblique or square tiles, or a building kit) to start a tile map from. Place and stack its tiles with place_map_tiles; add more groups there with add_group.

project_id.description: Attach the map to this game project. Without it the map exists but never syncs into a project workspace, so a game cannot load it.

tools.name: delete_map
tools.description:
Delete one of your maps. Immediate — there is no undo.

A map wired into a project is loaded by that project's game by id, so
deleting one that a game still references breaks that game's next build.
The response says how many projects referenced it.

map_id.description: The map to delete, from list_maps

tools.name: list_maps
tools.description:
List your maps, most recently edited first.

Pass `search` to find one by name — accounts reach four figures of maps, so
paging is not a way to look something up. Maps are made in PixelLab's Map
Workshop; use get_map to see one and edit_map to paint terrain on it.

search.description: Only maps whose name contains this (case-insensitive)

offset.description: Skip this many, to page deeper

tools.name: get_map
tools.description:
Show a map as an ASCII grid, one character per terrain cell.

With no crop you get the whole map downsampled to fit; pass x/y/width/height
for a 1:1 view of one area. Coordinates are terrain cells and can be
negative — the rulers show the real numbers, so read them off the view and
pass them straight to edit_map.

Maps built from tile groups (isometric, hex, oblique and similar tiles) show
their tile layers: for every cell the tile on top and the stack level it
sits on, plus each stacked column spelled out. Change those with
place_map_tiles.

export="godot" / "unity" / "pixellab" returns a download link for the map
as a game-engine project or the PixelLab ZIP instead of the view.

x.description: Crop: left edge, in terrain cells (q on tile layers)

y.description: Crop: top edge, in terrain cells (r on tile layers)

export.description: Instead of the view, get a download link for the map as Map Workshop's Export makes it: godot (Godot 4 project ZIP), unity (Unity 6 .unitypackage) or pixellab (PixelLab ZIP: map.json plus images, for custom engines). Free; the link needs no auth.

tools.name: edit_map
tools.description:
Paint terrain on a map: rivers and roads with `path`, areas with `rect`.

You choose regions, not tiles — the tileset picks the actual tile art for
every corner, and shoreline rows between terrains are inserted for you. Name
a terrain the map doesn't have yet and the tileset providing it is attached
automatically, along with any tileset connected to it. A tileset not
connected to this map attaches only when you name its terrain exactly; it
meets the map with hard edges (straight seams) until a tileset joins them.

On a sidescroller map each terrain is a platform top ("grass", "snow") over
its body, and empty cells are air: paint the solid ground. Naming a top the
map lacks attaches the sidescroller tileset that has it.

Cost: free. Painting spends no generations however much you repaint — the
tileset it draws with was paid for when it was generated.

Returns what changed, an ASCII view of the affected area, and — when the edit
used new art or went wrong — a rendered image of it. Pass show=true to see
the image any time; use view_map to look at somewhere you did not just paint.

oneOf.description: A stroke through waypoints — rivers, roads, coastlines.
An axis-aligned area — fields, plazas, blocks of ground.

dry_run.description: Preview the result and warnings without saving

show.description: Also return a rendered IMAGE of the edited area. On by default whenever the edit brings in a terrain you have not seen rendered, or leaves tiles no tileset can draw.

tools.name: view_map
tools.description:
Render the map to an image and return it, terrain and objects together.

Use this to judge how a map LOOKS — get_map's ASCII shows you where terrain
is, never what it looks like. Crop with x/y/width/height (the same cell
coordinates get_map and edit_map use) to inspect an area closely.

This renders from the terrain grid, so it always shows the map's CURRENT
state, including edits a human has not opened Map Workshop to see.
Sidescroller maps are not drawn: their side-view rules are not reproduced
here, so you get a note instead of a wrong picture.

x.description: Crop: left edge, in terrain cells

y.description: Crop: top edge, in terrain cells

tools.name: place_map_object
tools.description:
Place objects or characters on a map, at a terrain cell or an exact pixel.

Objects are how a map gets trees, houses, rocks and NPCs — terrain painting
(edit_map) only covers ground. A tileset tiles a SURFACE, so anything with a
silhouette has to be an object.

Position: x/y stands the sprite on that cell (the coordinates get_map
shows). world_x/world_y puts it at an exact world pixel instead, as Map
Workshop's free drag does — use it to match positions from a game scene or
an isometric layout that does not fall on the cell grid.

For many objects pass `placements`: one call, one save.

Returns a picture of the result by default, because a placement that is one
cell off, or far bigger than you expected, is invisible in text.

x.description: Terrain cell to stand the object on, as in get_map

y.description: Terrain cell to stand the object on, as in get_map

world_x.description: Exact position in world pixels, instead of x/y — the space of the map's object boundingBox and the game's sprites

anchor.description: What world_x/world_y name: 'foot' (default) = the sprite's bottom-centre; 'top_left' = the box origin, box_px in list_map_objects

direction.description: Facing for a character (south, north, east...). Leave unset for objects — most have a single sprite and it is picked automatically.

layer.description: Draw order; higher is on top. Defaults to the next layer.

placements.description: Place many in one call, instead of the single-placement arguments: [{"object_id":"…","x":3,"y":4}, {"object_id":"…","world_x":412,"world_y":230,"anchor":"foot"}, {"character_id":"…","x":1,"y":1,"direction":"south"}]. Each item takes the same fields as above. One save for all; if any item is invalid nothing is placed.

x.description: Terrain cell to stand it on

y.description: Terrain cell to stand it on

anchor.description: What world_x/world_y name: 'foot' (bottom-centre, default) or 'top_left' (the stored box origin, box_px in list_map_objects)

layer.description: Draw order; higher is on top

show.description: Return a rendered image of the placement

tools.name: place_map_tiles
tools.description:
Place, stack and erase tiles on a map's tile layers — the map editor's tile
painting, with its Stack layer control.

A map made from tile groups (isometric, hex, oblique, square tiles) keeps
each group as a tile layer; get_map lists them and shows, per cell, the
tile on top and its stack level. A cell holds a column of tiles: level 0
is the ground, and each level above sits one tile height higher, so a
`stack` of 3 builds a pillar and "on_top" builds on whatever is there.

Placing on a cell's level replaces the tile already there. As in the
editor, a tile placed on one ground layer clears that same cell and level
on any other ground layer drawn on the same grid.

Tiles go down exactly as given: for connected sets, pick the tile drawn
for that spot's neighbours (get_tiles_pro lists each tile's mask).

A building kit is several layers: floor, interior walls, outer walls, roof
(when the kit has roof pieces) and pieces (pillars, doorways, stairs). Lay
floor tiles and the outer walls follow the floor's outline. Interior walls
and roofs take no tile: each cell's piece follows its neighbours. A doorway
is cut into the wall at that cell, and stairs lay both halves. get_map lists
what each kit layer takes.

Returns what changed and a view of the area: the top tile and the top
level of every cell, and each stacked column level by level.

oneOf.description: Put one tile on cells, `stack` levels high.

layer.description: Tile layer index, as listed by get_map

area.description: An inclusive block of cells: q..q+width-1, r..r+height-1.

tile.description: Tile index in the layer's tile group. Left out on a building kit's interior-wall and roof layers, whose pieces follow their neighbours

oneOf.description: Remove tiles: everything from `level` up, or the top `stack` with on_top.

layer.description: Tile layer index, as listed by get_map

area.description: An inclusive block of cells: q..q+width-1, r..r+height-1.

oneOf.description: Lay another tile group on the map as new layers, after the existing ones.

tools.name: list_map_objects
tools.description:
List the objects and characters placed on a map, with their cell positions.

Gives you the placement id that move_map_object and remove_map_object take.
A placement id is per-PLACEMENT, not per-asset — the same tree placed twice
has two ids.

tools.name: move_map_object
tools.description:
Move a placed object or character to a different cell or an exact pixel, or
change its layer.

Keeps its sprite and refs. world_x/world_y positions it to the pixel, as Map
Workshop's free drag does; `layer` alone re-orders it without moving it.

x.description: Cell to stand it on, as in get_map

y.description: Cell to stand it on, as in get_map

world_x.description: Exact position in world pixels, instead of x/y

anchor.description: What world_x/world_y name: 'foot' (default) = the sprite's bottom-centre; 'top_left' = the box origin, box_px in list_map_objects

layer.description: New draw order (higher is on top). Pass it alone to change only the layer: the stored position, fractions included, is untouched.

show.description: Return a rendered image of the result

tools.name: remove_map_object
tools.description:
Remove placed objects or characters from a map.

Deletes placements only — the object or character itself is untouched and can
be placed again. Pass `placement_id` for one, or `asset_id` to clear every
placement of one asset at once.

asset_id.description: Remove EVERY placement of this object or character instead — the asset_id column in list_map_objects. Use it to clear one prop from a whole map in a single call.

tools.name: inpaint_map
tools.description:
Regenerate one rectangular area of a map with AI — a ramp, a broken wall, a
path through a forest, a seam between two terrains — the way Map Workshop's
inpainting does. Give the area in the same cells get_map and edit_map use.

Choosing the area: put what you want near its centre and make it a bit
larger than that, with a cell or two of the map you keep on every side. The
model blends the new pixels into what it sees at the area's edges; something
that runs into an edge (a stream, a wall) can end in a visible step where the
area stops.

The new pixels go into the map's inpainted layer, which sits over the
terrain and under objects, exactly where Map Workshop puts its own
inpainting; the terrain cells underneath are unchanged.

Cost: like inpaint_image_pro_flash, by the area's longest side in pixels — 5
generations up to 96px, 6 up to 208px, 9 up to 256px. Not available on
sidescroller maps or maps with tile layers (the area could not be drawn here
as Map Workshop shows it).

Non-blocking: returns a job_id. Poll inpaint_map(map_id=..., job_id=...);
when the job completes the result is written into the map (also
automatically) and the poll shows the area.

description.description: What the area should become, e.g. 'a wooden ramp from the shore up to the dock'. The model sees the map around it and continues its terrain, perspective and palette.

x.description: Area: left edge, in terrain cells

y.description: Area: top edge, in terrain cells

width.description: Area width in cells. 32-256px per side in multiples of 4px: 2-16 cells on a 16px map, 1-8 on a 32px map.

height.description: Area height in cells, as width

no_background.description: Keep only the new subject: its background is removed, so the terrain under the area shows through around it. Default False replaces the whole area, as Map Workshop does by default.

job_id.description: Poll an earlier inpaint_map call instead of starting one: reports progress, and once it is done makes sure the result is in the map and shows the area. Pass with map_id only.

tools.name: edit_map_areas
tools.description:
Declare what blocks movement, as Map Workshop's Gameplay Layers do.

Terrain says what a map LOOKS like; a gameplay layer says what it PLAYS
like. Without one the game falls back to reading the terrain's own names,
so a map is solid or open by accident of vocabulary.

A layer is linked to terrains rather than to an area: the exporter derives
the cells from the terrain grid every time the map is exported, so painting
more water extends the water layer by itself.

    edit_map_areas(map_id, action="add", name="Non-walkable",
                   terrains=["water"], walkable=false)

Call with no action to see the layers a map already has and what the game
makes of each one.

action.description: list the map's gameplay layers, or add/remove one

name.description: Layer name, for add and remove. The game reads the NAME as well as the tags, so name it for what it does: 'Non-walkable', 'Walkable'.

terrains.description: For add: the terrains this layer covers, by the names get_map shows (e.g. ["water","lava"]). The layer follows them — repaint the terrain and the collision follows, with no second edit here.

walkable.description: For add: true if the player can walk on these terrains, false if they block. Refused when the resulting layer would read the other way to the game, rather than writing one that plays wrong.

tools.name: rename_asset
tools.description:
Rename a character, object, tileset, map or UI asset, or one animation. Free, immediate.

Characters and objects carry two names: `name` is the asset's (what
list_characters / list_objects show, shared by every state) and
`state_name` is this state's own. Pass either or both. Characters also take
`description`, the text later animations and states are made from.

For an animation, pass the character/object id, its `animation_group_id`
and the new `name`; every direction of it is renamed.

asset_id.description: Id of your character, object, tileset, map or UI asset (from its list_* or get_* tool).

name.description: New name (max 120 characters). For a character/object this is the asset's name, shared by all its states. With animation_group_id it names that animation.

state_name.description: Characters/objects only: new name for this one state (e.g. 'Idle', 'armored').

description.description: Characters only: new character description. Animations and states made afterwards use it; existing art is unchanged.

animation_group_id.description: Rename one animation of the character/object instead: its [group: ...] id from get_character/get_object. Put the new name in `name`.

tools.name: manage_state
tools.description:
Copy a character or object state, or split it off into an asset of its own. Free.

duplicate: the copy gets the rotations, tags and project links, not the
animations, and is named after the source ('Idle (copy)', 'Idle (copy 2)'). Use
it to keep the original before editing a state with save_to_asset or
set_canvas_size. The source must be completed.

ungroup: the state keeps its id, own name, rotations and animations; the new
asset is named after the old one with the next copy number. A character/object
with one state has nothing to split off.

asset_id.description: Id of the character or object state.

action.description: duplicate: copy the state into a new state of the same asset. ungroup: remove the state from its character/object, making it an asset of its own.

tools.name: set_canvas_size
tools.description:
Change a character's or object's canvas size by adding or removing transparent margin. Free.

Every rotation is re-centred on the new canvas about its pivot. The art is
never scaled or cropped: a size smaller than the art itself is refused with
the art's bounds. Animations keep the canvas they were made on; an object's
map placements follow it. Use it to give a sprite room before animating
(a sword swing, a jump) or to trim empty margin.

width.description: New canvas width in px: a multiple of 4, 8-256 (objects: 8-400).

height.description: New canvas height in px: a multiple of 4, 8-256 (objects: 8-400).

tools.name: mirror_animation
tools.description:
Create an animation's missing opposite direction by flipping one horizontally. Free, immediate.

The flipped frames are added to the same animation (same animation_group_id)
as the opposite direction. Refused when that direction already exists:
delete it first with delete_animation(direction=...) to replace it. South and
north cannot be mirrored. Faster and free compared with generating the
direction, and exact for symmetric sprites; asymmetric details (a sword in
the right hand) end up in the other hand.

asset_id.description: Id of the character or object.

source_direction.description: Direction to flip. Creates its mirror: east <-> west, south-east <-> south-west, north-east <-> north-west.

tools.name: import_object
tools.description:
Import your own pixel art as a 1-direction object. Free, immediate.

The image becomes a completed object in your library, the same as uploading
it on the website: animate_object, create_object_state, set_canvas_size,
export_asset and place_map_object then work on it like on a generated one.
At most 256x256. Pixels are stored exactly; nothing is regenerated.

image_url.description: URL of the image: https, data:, or upload:<id> from get_upload_url. Preferred over image_base64 for anything but a tiny sprite.

tools.name: export_asset
tools.description:
Get a download link for a character or object as ZIP, spritesheet, .aseprite or GIF. Free.

The link needs no auth (the id is the key) and is fetched with plain HTTP,
e.g. `curl -fLo hero.aseprite <url>`. It answers 423 with Retry-After while
the asset or one of its animations is still generating.

tools.name: create_topdown_tileset
tools.description:
Generate a Wang tileset (corner-based autotiling) joining two terrains for a
top-down map. Returns a tileset id at once; poll get_topdown_tileset (standard
~30 s, pro a few minutes).

Modes: standard (default) is the website's standard tileset, cheap and fast,
16/24/32 px tiles. mode="pro" paints the richest tiles (textured ground, raised
banks, more shape controls), 16/32/64 px, Tier 1+: use it when the look
matters. transition_size sets the bank/wall height; a tall set has 25 tiles.

One tileset holds exactly two terrains; three or more need a chain: pass the
shared terrain's base tile id from get_topdown_tileset as the next set's
lower_base_tile_id/upper_base_tile_id. Standard redraws that terrain close, not
byte-identical; pro pastes it exactly. mode="pro" takes palette (plus
palette_name) or max_colors; standard takes neither.

Standard sometimes swaps the two terrains, far more often with grass as lower:
on a flat set put grass upper, and check each sheet's all-lower tile.

Cost: standard is 1 generation; mode="pro" costs 15 generations for tiles up
to 32 px, 25 above. Failed jobs are not charged.

Full reference (tile counts, shape controls, chaining, terrain order):
search_help(tool="create_topdown_tileset").

transition_size.description: Upper terrain height: 0 flat to 1.0 full-tile walls. Above 0.5 (pro: 0.5 and up) gives 25 tiles. Pro snaps to 0, 0.25, 0.5 or 1.0.

transition_description.description: The strip between the terrains, e.g. 'wet sand with foam'; used only when transition_size > 0.

tile_size.description: Square: {"width": N, "height": N} or a bare int N. 16, 24 or 32 for standard; 16, 32 or 64 for mode='pro'.

mode.description: "standard": cheap and fast. "pro": the richest painted tiles, needs a Tier 1+ plan (not a trial). See the tool description.

shape_style.description: Standard only (refused with pro): 'round' (the default) or 'square' border corners.

enhance.description: Standard only: AI-enhances the terrain descriptions before drawing; your own prompts are kept in metadata.

spread_x.description: No effect; kept so existing calls work.

slope_size.description: No effect; kept so existing calls work.

raggedness.description: Terrain boundary wobble, 0 = clean lines to 1 = rough. Both modes; tall pro sets (transition_size above 0.4) are half as rough. Omit for the generator's default: 0 on pro, 0.45 on standard (the website's Standard tab starts at 0).

side_wall_thickness.description: mode='standard', transition_size above 0. How thick the wall reads on the top rim and down both sides of the front face, 0-1 (transition_size sets the face depth). Omit for the default width (the website starts at 0.1).

side_wall_placement.description: mode='standard', transition_size above 0. Which side of the border the wall sits on: 0 = it sticks out past the terrain (the default when omitted), 1 = it is carved into the terrain so the shape stays put (the website starts at 0.5).

shape_seed.description: mode='standard'. Which wobble raggedness draws (0-99, the website's Reshuffle): another number gives a different boundary at the same raggedness.

lower_walkable.description: Whether the lower terrain can be walked on: true / false, or omit to leave it unstated (engine exports then guess from the terrain's name). Feeds the map and engine-export collision. Only for a terrain this tileset makes: a terrain reused through lower_base_tile_id keeps its own tileset's answer.

upper_walkable.description: Whether the upper terrain can be walked on: true / false, or omit to leave it unstated (engine exports then guess from the terrain's name). Feeds the map and engine-export collision. Only for a terrain this tileset makes: a terrain reused through upper_base_tile_id keeps its own tileset's answer.

roundness.description: Border corners: 0 square, 1 round, 2 cut at 45 degrees. Above 1 needs mode='pro'. Omit for the default.

boundary_amplitude.description: How far the border meanders (0 = straight). Pro, or standard with transition_size up to 0.5.

boundary_seed.description: Which meander boundary_amplitude draws; another number, another shape.

step_slope.description: Pro with transition_size 0.25 only: the bank from a cliff (0) to a gentle slope.

connect_diagonals.description: Pro only: true joins the two diagonal tiles' upper corners into one area.

outline.description: No effect; kept so existing calls work.

view.description: Pro only: match your characters' view (create_character defaults to low top-down). Standard always draws high top-down.

tile_strength.description: No effect; kept so existing calls work.

lower_base_tile_id.description: Chain: a base tile id from get_topdown_tileset (same tile size) reused as the lower terrain.

upper_base_tile_id.description: Chain: a base tile id from get_topdown_tileset (same tile size) reused as the upper terrain.

tileset_adherence.description: No effect; kept so existing calls work.

tileset_adherence_freedom.description: No effect; kept so existing calls work.

text_guidance_scale.description: No effect; kept so existing calls work.

palette.description: Target palette, 2 to 256 hex colours as a JSON array, e.g. ["#081820", "#346856", "#88c070", "#e0f8d0"] for Game Boy or ["#000000", "#ffffff"] for 1-bit. Every pixel the tool draws is one of them; pixels you supplied (a direction you drew) stay as they are.

palette_name.description: Optional name of the palette (e.g. 'Game Boy', 'PICO-8'); naming it helps the look. It only LABELS the colours you pass in palette rather than looking any up, so it cannot be sent on its own.

max_colors.description: At most this many colours (2-64). With a palette, they are picked from it. On the three tools that have a standard mode — create_character, create_topdown_tileset, animate_object — ANY palette setting needs mode='pro': standard refuses palette and max_colors, alone or together. Every other tool taking them has no standard mode and accepts them always.

tools.name: get_topdown_tileset
tools.description:
Get a topdown Wang tileset by ID. Returns status, download links, base tile IDs for chaining, and an example map image.

Download: no auth, the UUID is the key. GET /mcp/tilesets/{id}/image for the sheet PNG (add ?inline=true to be served the bytes instead of a CDN redirect, which Python stdlib clients need; ?layout=wang or ?layout=godot for the website download's Wang or Godot 3x3 arrangement), GET /mcp/tilesets/{id}/metadata for per-tile bounding_box (x/y/width/height, use as atlas regions), corners (NW/NE/SW/SE, each lower/upper/transition, use for Wang autotiling) and pattern_4x4. Both answer 423 + Retry-After while generating. Godot walkthrough: the MCP resource pixellab://docs/godot/wang-tilesets.

tileset_id.description: The UUID of the topdown tileset to retrieve

Use get_topdown_tileset(tileset_id) for full details.

tools.name: create_sidescroller_tileset
tools.description:
Generate a sidescroller tileset for 2D platformer games with side-view perspective.

This tool starts an asynchronous tileset generation that returns immediately with a tileset ID.
Use get_sidescroller_tileset to check status and retrieve the completed tileset.

Which mode: standard (default) is the website's standard sidescroller tileset
(pixen, side view), cheap and fast. mode="pro" paints the richest platforms;
use it when the look matters, standard when cost does.

Cost: standard is 1 generation now that it runs on pixen. (The classic model
it replaced billed 2 or 3 generations — NOT 1, over 1,186 prod charges, mean
2.6.) mode="pro" costs 15 generations for tiles up to 32 px and 25 above
that — the same ladder top-down pro uses, since both read one price(). Failed jobs are
not charged.

Creates tilesets optimized for 2D platformer games:
- Side-view perspective (not top-down)
- Transparent background (no background terrain)
- Platform/ground tiles with flat surfaces (no slopes)
- Optional decorative transition layer on top of base terrain

Use case: Building 2D platformer games with seamless terrain tiles.

## Creating Connected Tilesets

Use base tile IDs to create multiple tilesets that seamlessly connect:

1. Create first tileset (e.g., stone platform, either mode) and wait for completion
2. Use get_sidescroller_tileset to retrieve the base tile ID
3. Pass that base tile ID with mode="pro" to create the next tileset

Chaining needs mode="pro": standard draws the new top around every edge of a
chained platform instead of only on top.

The base tile is the platform body: chaining reuses it and draws a new top.
Example workflow:
- Tileset 1: stone brick platform, grass on top → get base tile ID
- Tileset 2: stone brick platform, snow on top (stone base tile ID, mode="pro")
- Tileset 3: stone brick platform, moss on top (same base tile ID, mode="pro")

A different body (wood, metal) is a new tileset without base_tile_id.

platform_thickness (standard only) sets how thick the platforms are, as the
website's Platform Thickness slider; omitted, it adapts to transition_size.

Generation time: standard ~30 seconds, pro a few minutes (async processing)

transition_size.description: Size of terrain transition. Controls how much of the surface layer appears (0.0 = no surface layer, 0.25 = light surface layer, 0.5 = heavy surface layer). Snapped to the nearest of 0, 0.25 and 0.5.

mode.description: Pro needs a Tier 1+ plan (not a trial). "standard": the website's standard sidescroller tileset (pixen, side view), cheap and fast. "pro": the richest platforms - painted texture, a cleaner cap - use it when the look matters.

enhance.description: mode='standard' only. AI-enhances the platform and surface descriptions and picks matching base colours before generation. The stored tileset keeps the enhanced text; your original prompts are kept in its metadata.

tile_size.description: Tile dimensions as {"width": N, "height": N}, OR a bare int N for a square tile (same shape create_tiles_pro accepts). 16 or 32 pixels.

platform_thickness.description: mode='standard' only. How thick the platform body is, 0 = thin to 1 = thick; omit to adapt it to transition_size (the website's 'auto').

outline.description: No effect: standard runs on pixen and pro ignores it; kept so existing calls work.

tile_strength.description: No effect: standard runs on pixen and pro ignores it; kept so existing calls work.

base_tile_id.description: mode='pro' only. base_tile_id from get_sidescroller_tileset: the platform body is reused, so describe the same body in lower_description and the new top in transition_description

tileset_adherence.description: No effect: standard runs on pixen and pro ignores it; kept so existing calls work.

tileset_adherence_freedom.description: No effect: standard runs on pixen and pro ignores it; kept so existing calls work.

text_guidance_scale.description: No effect: standard runs on pixen and pro ignores it; kept so existing calls work.

tools.description:
Get a sidescroller tileset by ID. Returns status, download links, and tile count.
Sidescroller tilesets are for 2D platformer games with transparent backgrounds.

tileset_id.description: ID of the sidescroller tileset to retrieve

tools.name: list_sidescroller_tilesets
tools.description:
List your sidescroller (platformer) tilesets. One line per tileset with status.
Use get_sidescroller_tileset(tileset_id) for full details.

limit.description: Maximum number of tilesets to return
