tools.name: create_map_object
tools.description:
Create a pixel art object with transparent background. ~30-90s. Returns an
ordinary object ID immediately: place_map_object puts it on a map,
animate_object gives it an ambient loop (it has one direction, so it animates
that single facing), get_object and get_map_object both read it. Nothing has
to be re-created with create_1_direction_object to be animated — that pays
10-15 generations again for an object you already own.

Two modes:
- Basic (no background_image): standalone object from description. Requires width/height.
- Style matching (with background_image): matches your map's art style. Width/height auto-detected.
  Default inpainting: oval 60%. Options: oval, rectangle, or custom mask.

Canvas: 32-400px. Basic max 400x400, inpainting max 192x192.
Transparency: the background is transparent up to 40,000px area (200x200, e.g.
128x256, 192x192); larger basic-mode canvases get a flat single-colour one.
background_image: {"type": "base64", "base64": "..."} (file paths not supported)
inpainting: {"type": "oval", "fraction": 0.3} | {"type": "rectangle", "fraction": 0.5} | {"type": "mask", "mask_image": "base64..."}

Use get_map_object to check status. The object is permanent and can be
placed on a map with place_map_object.

description.description: Object description (e.g., 'wooden barrel', 'stone fountain')

width.description: Canvas width in pixels (required for basic mode, auto-detected from background_image if provided)

height.description: Canvas height in pixels (required for basic mode, auto-detected from background_image if provided)

background_image.description: Background image for style matching (optional). Format: {"type": "base64", "base64": "..."}. File paths are not supported (server cannot read local files). If provided without inpainting config, uses default: oval 60%.

inpainting.description: Inpainting configuration as JSON string (optional). DEFAULT: If background_image provided but this omitted, uses oval 0.6. Options: {"type": "oval", "fraction": 0.3} for auto oval mask, {"type": "rectangle", "fraction": 0.5} for auto rectangle mask, {"type": "mask", "mask_image": "base64..."} for custom mask. Mask convention: WHITE (255) = area where AI generates, BLACK (0) = frozen/preserved context. Fraction is 0.05-0.95 (how much of background the shape covers).

tools.name: get_map_object
tools.description:
Get map object status and data. Returns image if completed.
The object is permanent — place it on a map with place_map_object.
Retries saving finished pixels when B2 or database persistence failed.

tools.name: create_1_direction_object
tools.description:
Queue a 1-direction object (10 or 15 generations, ~2-3 min). Returns object_id
immediately.

When size ≤170, produces multiple candidates (4/16/64) in 'review' status.
Call get_object to view candidates as inline images, then:
- select_object_frames(object_id, indices=[...]) to keep specific ones
- dismiss_review(object_id) to discard all
Single candidates are kept automatically.

For a fixed palette (Game Boy, PICO-8, any palette from Lospec) pass `palette`
as its hex colours: objects are drawn for them and every pixel is one of them.

Cost: 10 or 15 generations — NEVER 25, because this tool stops at 256px and the
25 band is out of reach. You pay the tier of the whole candidate sheet (your
canvas times the candidates per side), so the price is not monotonic in size:
going one step UP near a boundary can be the cheaper call. Each band with its
own price, ascending: 10 for 16-32; 15 for 33-42; 10 for 43-64; 15 for 65-85;
10 for 86-128; 15 for 129-170; 10 for 171-256. The receipt reports what was
actually charged.

description.description: Object description (e.g., 'wooden barrel', 'forest mushroom')

size.description: Square image size in pixels (min 16, max 256). Defaults to 64 when omitted. Cannot be set together with style_images — when style_images are provided, the largest style image determines the output size. The effective size also determines how many candidate objects are produced in one shot (≤42→64, ≤85→16, ≤170→4, else 1). Multi-object results enter 'review' status — call get_object to inspect, then select_object_frames or dismiss_review to finalize.

name.description: Object name for reference (e.g., 'wooden barrel', 'Forest Mushroom'). Defaults to the description when omitted.

view.description: View. NOTE: 1-direction uses top-down/sidescroller; create_8_direction_object and create_map_object use a different set (low top-down / high top-down / side).

style_images.description: Style reference images, PNG/JPEG base64 (max 256x256 px each). Each image: {"base64": "<png-data>", "format": "png"}. The maximum count depends on `size`: ≤85 → 8, ≤170 → 4, else → 1. When empty, a default style is used based on `view`. Output stays square at the style image's longer side: a 48x96 style image gives 96x96 candidates. For a non-square sprite (48x96 furniture) create_image_pro takes width and height. Note: this is NOT the same as reference_image on tileset tools (which is a small 16x16/32x32 texture).

item_descriptions.description: Per-object descriptions when `size` produces multiple objects. Length must not exceed the object count derived from `size`. Supplying FEWER is allowed and does NOT shrink the grid: the remaining slots are generated from `description`, so they come back as extra objects in the same style, not as variations of the items you listed. One description at size=48 therefore returns 16 objects, only the first of which is the one you named.

palette.description: Target palette, 2 to 256 hex colours as a JSON array, e.g. ["#081820", "#346856", "#88c070", "#e0f8d0"] for Game Boy or ["#000000", "#ffffff"] for 1-bit. Every pixel the tool draws is one of them; pixels you supplied (a direction you drew) stay as they are.

palette_name.description: Optional name of the palette (e.g. 'Game Boy', 'PICO-8'); naming it helps the look. It only LABELS the colours you pass in palette rather than looking any up, so it cannot be sent on its own.

max_colors.description: At most this many colours (2-64). With a palette, they are picked from it. On the three tools that have a standard mode — create_character, create_topdown_tileset, animate_object — ANY palette setting needs mode='pro': standard refuses palette and max_colors, alone or together. Every other tool taking them has no standard mode and accepts them always.

tools.name: create_8_direction_object
tools.description:
Queue an 8-direction object rendered from 8 angles (10-25 generations, ~2-4 min).
Returns object_id immediately. Use get_object to check status.
For single-direction objects, use create_1_direction_object instead.
For a console or palette look (1-bit, Game Boy, PICO-8, any Lospec palette) pass
`palette` as its hex colours plus `palette_name`: all 8 directions are drawn for
it and every pixel is one of its colours.

Cost: 168px per side is the hard maximum here — a bigger frame is refused
before anything is charged, and create_1_direction_object is the one that
reaches 256 (on its own, differently shaped ladder; do not read its bands
here). Within 168, the price follows the frame's LONGEST side, since all 8
angles share one sheet: 10 generations up to 84px; 15 for 85 to 112; 25 for
113 to 168 — so 64x64 is 10, 96x96 is 15, 120x120 is 25 and 128x128 is 25.
This ladder only ever climbs.

description.description: Object description (e.g., 'wooden barrel', 'stone fountain')

size.description: Square image size in pixels (min 24, max 168 — below 24 the eight angles stop being distinguishable, so use create_1_direction_object for 16px). Defaults to 64 when omitted. Cannot be set together with reference_image_base64 or style_image_base64 — in those cases the image dimensions determine the output size. The finished canvas is padded to fit the generation grid, so it can be larger than requested (34x34 for 32, 85x85 for 69); get_object reports the final size.

name.description: Object name for reference (e.g., 'Treasure Chest', 'Oak Barrel'). Defaults to the description when omitted.

reference_image_base64.description: Reference image of an OBJECT/item — generates 8 rotations from it. Works well for props (barrels, chests). NOTE: identity transfer is unreliable for CHARACTER/humanoid sprites — the reference sits in the center of a grid of placeholder characters and can lose the salience contest, so the output may resemble a generic character instead. For a character sprite, use create_character(mode="v3", reference_image_base64=...) instead — that pipeline reproduces the input faithfully. Mutually exclusive with style_image_base64.

style_image_base64.description: Style reference — generates a new object matching the description with the style of this image. Mutually exclusive with reference_image_base64.

style_object_id.description: ID of one of your existing 8-direction objects to use as the style reference. Its 8 directional sprites guide the new object's style in every direction. The style object must be completed with 8 directions, and size must be at least its sprite content size — the job fails fast with the required size otherwise.

palette.description: Target palette, 2 to 256 hex colours as a JSON array, e.g. ["#081820", "#346856", "#88c070", "#e0f8d0"] for Game Boy or ["#000000", "#ffffff"] for 1-bit. Every pixel the tool draws is one of them; pixels you supplied (a direction you drew) stay as they are.

palette_name.description: Optional name of the palette (e.g. 'Game Boy', 'PICO-8'); naming it helps the look. It only LABELS the colours you pass in palette rather than looking any up, so it cannot be sent on its own.

max_colors.description: At most this many colours (2-64). With a palette, they are picked from it. On the three tools that have a standard mode — create_character, create_topdown_tileset, animate_object — ANY palette setting needs mode='pro': standard refuses palette and max_colors, alone or together. Every other tool taking them has no standard mode and accepts them always.

tools.name: get_object
tools.description:
Get object details. Branches by status:
- processing: progress + ETA
- review: candidate frame URLs + inline previews
- expanding / review-expansion: an 8-direction expansion
  (expand_object_to_8_directions) running, then waiting to be kept or discarded
- completed: rotation URLs, animations, download link
- failed: error + retry hint

Download: `/mcp/objects/{id}/download` is a ZIP holding
`rotations/<direction>.png` and
`animations/<name>/<direction>/frame_000.png` (frame_NNN, 3 digits, from
000) at the ZIP root — flatter than the character ZIP, and with no
metadata.json. A one-direction object with no animations comes back as a
bare PNG instead of a ZIP. `/mcp/objects/{id}/spritesheet` is a ZIP of one
sheet PNG + layout JSON: one row per animation-direction, uniform cells
sized to the largest frame (nothing resized), `pivot: "cell-center"`.
To get an animation's pixels INLINE, with no download and nothing charged:
`pixelart_workbench(argv=["inspect", "object:<id>:<direction>:<animation>"])`
returns its frames as one sheet image in the tool result. A one-direction
object still needs the direction, and it is the literal `unknown` —
`object:<id>:unknown:<group id>`. `join ref ref --as rows` lays several
animations out one per row (at most 1024 px a side).

include_preview.description: Embed preview image (south for 8-dir, candidates for review).

tools.name: list_objects
tools.description:
List your objects with status and progress. One line per object.
Use get_object(object_id) for full details.

tags.description: Comma-separated tags to filter by (matches ANY tag).

status_filter.description: Filter by status: completed, review, pending, processing, failed, expanding, review-expansion (an 8-direction expansion running, then waiting to be kept or discarded).

search.description: Filter by name, case-insensitive. Matches the name shown here and the description it was created from, so 'chest' finds 'treasure chest'.

tools.name: animate_object
tools.description:
Add an animation to an existing, completed object. Returns one queued job per
direction at once (~30-60s each, pixminimax ~1-7 min). Poll with get_object.

For a character (create_character) use animate_character; for an image that is
not a PixelLab object, animate_image.

Modes:
- v3 (default): from animation_description; usually best and cheapest.
- pixminimax (beta): longer clips, frames a multiple of 4 up to 40.
- pro: a different style. Its first call returns the price; re-call with
  confirm_cost=True only after the user agrees.

1-direction objects animate their one facing; 8-direction objects all 8 unless
you pass directions. To add directions to an animation, pass its
animation_group_id (from get_object) and the mode it was made with. A start or
end frame needs exactly one direction. Palette is pro only;
max_colors is Pro-only too.

Cost: v3 ceil(width x height x frames / 65536) per direction, minimum 1: 48x48
or 64x64 at 8 frames = 1, 96x96, 128x96 or 128x128 = 2; width x height x frames
is capped at 524,288. pixminimax: 64x64 at 4/8/16/40 frames = 1/1/2/6 per
direction. pro: 10-25 per direction (80-200 for all 8).

Full reference (frame rules per mode, keyframes, direction prompts):
search_help(tool="animate_object").

object_id.description: Object UUID to animate (must be a completed object).

mode.description: v3 (default) is usually best and cheapest. Adding directions to an animation_group_id: pass the mode it was made with (others are refused).

animation_description.description: The motion, e.g. 'walking cheerfully'. Required for a new animation; inherited when adding directions via animation_group_id.

directions.description: 8-direction objects only (a 1-direction object refuses it). Omit for all 8, or, with animation_group_id, for the ones it is missing.

frame_count.description: Omit for the mode's default (8; pro: the smallest its canvas allows). v3: even, 4-16. pixminimax: a multiple of 4, 4-40. pro: 16 up to 64px, 4/9/16 up to 128px, 9 up to 170px.

animation_group_id.description: An existing animation's id (from get_object) to add directions to it; omit to start a new one (its id is returned).

display_name.description: Optional name for the animation, shown in the UI and used when exporting.

replace_existing.description: True to regenerate a direction this animation already has; otherwise that is refused.

confirm_cost.description: pro only. Never true on the first call, which returns the cost to show the user; re-call with true only after they confirm.

custom_start_frame_base64.description: v3/pixminimax: a start pose instead of the object's idle frame; its size sets the canvas (max 256x256). 8-direction objects: ONE direction, the one the user names (ask; never pick one).

end_frame_base64.description: v3/pixminimax: a pose to animate toward, same size as the start frame. One direction, as for custom_start_frame_base64.

keep_first_frame.description: v3/pixminimax: keep the start frame as frame 0 (frame_count + 1 stored); false stores exactly frame_count.

direction_prompts.description: v3/pixminimax, 8-direction objects: one description per direction, all eight keys; animation_description may then be left out. Reused when adding directions to the animation.

palette.description: Target palette, 2 to 256 hex colours as a JSON array, e.g. ["#081820", "#346856", "#88c070", "#e0f8d0"] for Game Boy or ["#000000", "#ffffff"] for 1-bit. Every pixel the tool draws is one of them; pixels you supplied (a direction you drew) stay as they are.

palette_name.description: Optional name of the palette (e.g. 'Game Boy', 'PICO-8'); naming it helps the look. It only LABELS the colours you pass in palette rather than looking any up, so it cannot be sent on its own.

max_colors.description: At most this many colours (2-64). With a palette, they are picked from it. On the three tools that have a standard mode — create_character, create_topdown_tileset, animate_object — ANY palette setting needs mode='pro': standard refuses palette and max_colors, alone or together. Every other tool taking them has no standard mode and accepts them always.

tools.name: create_object_state
tools.description:
Queue a state (variant) of an existing object. Auto-waits up to 30s for the
source object to complete. Returns a new object ID grouped with the source
via group_id.

An object is a group of states: `name` is the object's name (shared by all
states), and each state has its own `state_name` — defaulting to the edit
description truncated to 20 characters (a new object's first state is named
"base"). Pass `state_name` to name the new state explicitly.

A state is the SAME object in another condition (open/closed, lit, broken).
A different item belongs in its own object — for a matching look, pass the
source's image as style_images to create_1_direction_object. States move
together: adding or removing one in a project or folder moves every state.

`palette` (hex colours, plus `palette_name`) puts the state, every direction of
it, on those colours; the source goes on them before the edit.

Cost: known before the call, and the receipt repeats it. It is ONE charge for
the whole state, covering every direction the source has — there is no
per-direction price. An 8-direction state edited from text goes by the
frame's LONGEST side — 10 generations up
to 84px, 15 from 85 to 112, 25 above. Every other state (a 1-direction
object, or any state given a reference image) is priced like the other
canvas tools: 10 up to a square 256x256, 15 to 341x341, 25 above, measured
at the frame's own aspect ratio rather than its longest side.

object_id.description: Source object UUID to create a state of

state_name.description: Name for the new state (e.g. 'Mossy', 'Golden'). Defaults to the edit description truncated to 20 characters.

palette.description: Target palette, 2 to 256 hex colours as a JSON array, e.g. ["#081820", "#346856", "#88c070", "#e0f8d0"] for Game Boy or ["#000000", "#ffffff"] for 1-bit. Every pixel the tool draws is one of them; pixels you supplied (a direction you drew) stay as they are.

palette_name.description: Optional name of the palette (e.g. 'Game Boy', 'PICO-8'); naming it helps the look. It only LABELS the colours you pass in palette rather than looking any up, so it cannot be sent on its own.

max_colors.description: At most this many colours (2-64). With a palette, they are picked from it. On the three tools that have a standard mode — create_character, create_topdown_tileset, animate_object — ANY palette setting needs mode='pro': standard refuses palette and max_colors, alone or together. Every other tool taking them has no standard mode and accepts them always.

tools.name: delete_object
tools.description:
Permanently delete an object, its rotations/frames, animations, tags,
project assignments, and storage files. Immediate — this cannot be undone.

tools.name: update_object_tags
tools.description:
Replace ALL tags on an object (set operation, free, synchronous).

Tags organize and filter objects — see list_objects(tags=...). Passing an
empty list clears every tag. This replaces the full set: include existing
tags you want to keep.

object_id.description: Object UUID whose tags to replace

tags.description: Full replacement tag list (max 20 tags, 50 chars each; whitespace trimmed, case-insensitive dedup). Empty list clears all tags.

tools.name: select_object_frames
tools.description:
Promote selected frames of a review object to individual completed objects.

See get_object on a review-status object to view candidates inline.
Each selected index becomes its own 1-direction object. Once no frames
remain in the review object it is deleted automatically. If a call times
out it may still finish: check get_object before retrying (promoted frames
leave the review object, and re-selecting one is refused).

On an 8-direction expansion review (expand_object_to_8_directions, status
review-expansion), call it with no indices to keep the expansion: the same
object becomes 8-direction, its canvas grows to the review's size and its
animations move to the expansion's existing direction.

indices.description: 0-based indices of frames to keep. Each becomes a separate completed 1-direction object. Leave out on an 8-direction expansion review (status review-expansion): that keeps all 8 directions.

common_tag.description: Optional tag applied to every newly-created object.

tools.name: dismiss_review
tools.description:
Discard a review-status object and delete all its candidate frames.
Used when none of the consistent-style candidates are worth keeping.

On an 8-direction expansion (expand_object_to_8_directions, status expanding
or review-expansion) it discards only the new directions: the object itself
is kept, unchanged and 1-direction.

tools.name: expand_object_to_8_directions
tools.description:
Turn one of your 1-direction objects into an 8-direction one, keeping the
same object: its id, tags and animations. Costs 10-25 generations by the
padded canvas (objects up to 168x168; larger ones are refused), ~2-4 min.

The new directions wait for review. get_object shows them (status
review-expansion) and the object stays 1-direction until you decide:
select_object_frames(object_id) with no indices keeps them (the canvas grows
to the review's size, animations move to existing_direction);
dismiss_review(object_id) discards them and leaves the object as it was.

To make a NEW 8-direction object from an image instead, use
create_8_direction_object(reference_image_base64=...).

object_id.description: Your completed 1-direction object (from list_objects or get_object).

existing_direction.description: Which way the object's current image faces. That image becomes this direction, unchanged, and the other 7 are drawn to match it. Ask the user if the image does not make it clear.

description.description: What the object is, to guide the new angles. Defaults to the object's own description.

tools.name: create_ui_asset
tools.description:
Queue a pixel-art UI panel (10-25 generations, ~2-4 min). Returns ui_asset_id immediately.
Omit `pieces` for a default rounded-rect panel. Use get_ui_asset to check status.
For a fixed palette (Game Boy, PICO-8, any palette from Lospec) pass `palette` as
its hex colours: the panel is drawn for them and every pixel is one of them.

Cost: 10 generations for a canvas up to 256x256, 15 up to 341x341, 25 above
— so the 256x256 default is the cheap option and 512x512 is 25. A non-square
panel is measured at its own aspect ratio, which is more generous than its
longer side: a 16:9 panel is 10 up to 341x192, 15 to 456x256, 25 from 457
wide. There is no quote endpoint; the response reports the actual charge.

description.description: Style of the UI panel (e.g. 'wooden RPG panel with gold trim')

width.description: Output width in px (192–688). Max is aspect-gated, NOT freely combinable: square ≤512×512, 16:9 ≤688×384, 9:16 ≤384×688, 4:3 ≤600×448, 3:4 ≤448×600. E.g. 688×512 is rejected (resolves to 4:3, max 600×448) — use 688×384 or 512×512.

height.description: Output height in px (192–688). Max is aspect-gated (see width): the two axis maxes cannot be combined — 688 only with a 16:9/9:16 partner (688×384 or 384×688), 512 only as a square (512×512).

palette.description: Target palette, 2 to 256 hex colours as a JSON array, e.g. ["#081820", "#346856", "#88c070", "#e0f8d0"] for Game Boy or ["#000000", "#ffffff"] for 1-bit. Every pixel the tool draws is one of them; pixels you supplied (a direction you drew) stay as they are.

palette_name.description: Optional name of the palette (e.g. 'Game Boy', 'PICO-8'); naming it helps the look. It only LABELS the colours you pass in palette rather than looking any up, so it cannot be sent on its own.

max_colors.description: At most this many colours (2-64). With a palette, they are picked from it. On the three tools that have a standard mode — create_character, create_topdown_tileset, animate_object — ANY palette setting needs mode='pro': standard refuses palette and max_colors, alone or together. Every other tool taking them has no standard mode and accepts them always.

style_image_base64.description: Optional style reference image (base64 PNG/JPEG, ideally <=1024px per side). The panel matches its palette, pixel scale, outlines and shading — the strongest way to make UI fit an existing game. Only the art style is copied, never its content or layout.

name.description: Friendly name for the saved asset

project_id.description: Optional PixelLab project ID to assign the finished UI asset to

elements.description: Named UI element types to scaffold the panel from (auto-positioned, no coords needed). Available: button, icon_button, toolbar, tab, panel, window, health_bar, avatar, triangle, pentagon, hexagon, octagon. Combine with `pieces` for custom shapes; omit both for a default panel.

pieces.description: Advanced shape template (validated). Each piece needs a unique `id`, a `kind`, and an optional `label`. Allowed kinds: rounded_rect {x,y,w,h,radius}, circle {x,y,r}, polygon {x,y,r,sides,phase}. Coords are on a virtual editor canvas — longer side 0–512, shorter side scaled to the output aspect (a 16:9 panel uses a 512×288 coordinate grid, not the output size). Omit for a default full-canvas panel.

anyOf.description:
Regular polygon — `sides` vertices at distance `r` from (x, y),
starting from angle `phase` (radians).

tools.name: list_jobs
tools.description:
List your active background jobs (pending + processing).

Use this to find stuck jobs you can cancel with cancel_job.

include_recent.description: Include recently completed/failed jobs (last 30 min). Default: only active jobs.

tools.name: get_ui_asset
tools.description:
Get a UI asset. Processing → progress; completed → image URL + download links.

A template lists the elements split from it (each with its states), or, not
split yet, where update_ui_asset(split=True) would cut it. An element lists its states and
any create_ui_states job still making them. Also the 9-slice, and for a
template a ZIP link with every PNG + metadata.json.

tools.name: list_ui_assets
tools.description:
List your UI panels with status. One line per asset.
Use get_ui_asset(ui_asset_id) for full details.

tools.name: delete_ui_asset
tools.description:
Permanently delete a UI panel (and, for a template, its split elements + their
states) plus the backing image files. Immediate — this cannot be undone.

tools.name: create_ui_states
tools.description:
Make states for UI elements (split from a template with update_ui_asset(split=True)): hover,
pressed, disabled, selected, or anything you describe. Each becomes a UI asset
of kind state under its element, in the same art. Returns a job id at once
(~1-2 min); wait_for_jobs, then get_ui_asset lists them. Each state is trimmed
to what it draws (glow included), so it can be smaller than its element's
canvas: centre it on the element's drawn part.

One generation draws every element in every state on one labelled grid, so a
set stays consistent. Priced by that grid's side (each element plus an 18 px
margin, a 24 px label per state): 10 generations up to 256 px, 15 up to 341,
25 above. One 64x24 button in hover + pressed is 10; two 96x32 buttons in the
same two states are 15. Charged when the states are saved.

element_ids.description: Elements to make the states for: ids from update_ui_asset(split=True) / get_ui_asset(template). All of them in one generation, so the states match across them.

states.description: The states every element gets, e.g. [{"name": "hover", "description": "brighter, a soft glow on the rim"}, {"name": "pressed", "description": "pushed in: darker, face 1 px lower"}]

name.description: The state's name, e.g. hover, pressed, disabled, selected

description.description: How the element looks in this state, e.g. 'pushed in: darker, the face one pixel lower'

palette.description: Target palette, 2 to 256 hex colours as a JSON array, e.g. ["#081820", "#346856", "#88c070", "#e0f8d0"] for Game Boy or ["#000000", "#ffffff"] for 1-bit. Every pixel the tool draws is one of them; pixels you supplied (a direction you drew) stay as they are.

palette_name.description: Optional name of the palette (e.g. 'Game Boy', 'PICO-8'); naming it helps the look. It only LABELS the colours you pass in palette rather than looking any up, so it cannot be sent on its own.

max_colors.description: At most this many colours (2-64). With a palette, they are picked from it. On the three tools that have a standard mode — create_character, create_topdown_tileset, animate_object — ANY palette setting needs mode='pro': standard refuses palette and max_colors, alone or together. Every other tool taking them has no standard mode and accepts them always.

tools.name: update_ui_asset
tools.description:
Edit a UI asset, free (nothing is generated). One change per call:

- split=True: cut a template into elements, each its own UI asset (PNG) to place,
  9-slice, give hover/pressed states (create_ui_states) and download.
  get_ui_asset(template id) shows where it cuts first. To split differently,
  delete its elements first. Editing or deleting an element re-composes the
  template's image from its elements.
- nine_slice / clear_nine_slice: the border insets that stay crisp when a panel,
  button or bar is stretched to another size in a game. Stored with the asset:
  get_ui_asset, its ZIP's metadata.json and the /chat game's assets/ui/index.json
  carry it.

To rename a UI asset, use rename_asset.

ui_asset_id.description: UI asset id: a template, element or state

split.description: Split this TEMPLATE into elements: each button, bar, frame or icon in it becomes its own UI asset. A template splits once.

split_boxes.description: With split: your own crop boxes in template pixels, [{"label": "Play", "x": 40, "y": 30, "width": 120, "height": 40}, ...]: e.g. the boxes get_ui_asset lists with one moved. Omit to cut along the shapes the template was generated from. At most 64.

items.description: One element's crop box, in the template image's pixels.

nine_slice.description: 9-slice insets in the asset's own pixels, {"left": 6, "right": 6, "top": 6, "bottom": 6}: the borders that stay crisp when the image is stretched; left + right below its width, top + bottom below its height.

tools.name: create_room
tools.description:
Paint one room (a 7 x 6 grid of 32 px floor cells; top-down 256x256 px, or isometric) as pixel
art, built and furnished for its theme (a castle's, a house's, a starship's), its doorways
where `doors` puts them so rooms join up on a map; the rock round its walls is transparent.
A top-down room's building kit can also come as a 16, 24, 48 or 64 px tileset (tile_size).
Takes ~4 minutes (1 in 10 over 8); returns a room id at once.
Costs 20 generations when the room is ready (25 with tile_size 48 or 64; 10 more for its
pieces). Needs Tier 1 (Pixel Apprentice) or higher.

theme.description: What the room is, in one line: what it is and where decide its walls, floor and furniture (e.g. "The bridge of a starship.", "A blacksmith's forge under a castle.")

doors.description: The doors, 1-8 of {"side": "n"|"e"|"s"|"w", "col": 0-6, "row": 0-5}: n = a door in a back wall (the wall above a floor cell), e/w = an open doorway in the right/left wall beside a cell (two cells tall: `row` is the upper one), s = an open doorway in the bottom wall below a cell. Each must sit on a wall of the floor, and an e/w doorway needs two cells of wall between it and an inner corner below it. Example for the full room: [{"side": "s", "col": 3, "row": 5}, {"side": "w", "col": 0, "row": 2}]

cells.description: The floor plan, seen from above: 6 rows of 7 characters, '#' floor and '.' solid rock, the floor in one piece. Left out: the whole 7 x 6 grid is floor. An L-shaped room: ["####...", "####...", "#######", "#######", "#######", "#######"]

name.description: Optional name; named from the theme when left out.

pieces.description: Also cut the furniture out as movable pieces, each with its own shadow, to move, remove or reuse in the website's room editor (~5-8 more minutes, charged on its own). Only when the user wants to rearrange the furniture: the painted room is complete without it, and cut_out_room_furniture does it later.

style_room_id.description: A style room: another of the user's finished rooms (its room_id) whose look the new room takes (the same walls, wall tops, floor, door, wall lights and hanging), so rooms of one building join up. The shape (cells, doors) and the furniture are the new room's own; `theme` then says what this room is ("its kitchen"). It must be in the same view as the new room.

style_room_floor.description: With style_room_id: take the style room's floor too. False gives the new room its own floor, decided by `theme` ("its chapel, with a wooden floor"), under the style room's walls, wall tops, door, wall lights and hanging.

view.description: top-down: the back walls' faces show above the floor (256x256 px). isometric: 2:1 isometric, the n and w walls tall with their doors in them, the s and e walls low curbs with open doorways; the same cells and doors, a picture of about 248x176 px for the full grid. oblique: the floor a square grid seen from above, heights leaning up and to the left, the n and w walls tall, the s and e walls low curbs; walls, doors and floor only, no furniture yet (pieces must be false); about 272x240 px for the full grid.

project_id.description: A project of yours to file the room in (list_projects); a game also uses it, so a Game Builder workspace gets it under assets/rooms/{room_id}/. Left out: your auto-add setting.

tile_size.description: Top-down rooms only: the tile size of the tileset its building kit comes as. 32 is the room's own; 16, 24, 48 or 64 also paints the kit at that size, so the kit download (get_room's `building kit (zip)`) holds a tileset-15 sheet and its metadata at that size too. The room's picture stays 32 px cells. 48 or 64 costs 25 generations instead of 20.

tools.name: get_room
tools.description:
A room's state. While it is being made: its stage and progress. When ready: the room
as painted (inline), its download link and its building kit's (a ZIP of the wall, door
and floor tiles it was built from); once its furniture is cut out
(cut_out_room_furniture), its movable pieces by name and the link that opens it in the
website's room editor (move, remove or bring in pieces; shadows follow).

Download: the room as painted is the `download:` PNG. Its cut-out pieces and its
furniture-free floor are in the `layers:` JSON this prints once the pieces are ready
(public, no auth) — you do not need the editor to export them. Keys: `w`/`h` the
room's pixel size; `room` the painting as you see it; `lit` and `unlit` the SAME room
with every piece removed (the empty floor, lit and unlit); `sprites[]` one entry per
piece with `name`, `x`,`y` (its top-left in those pixels), `foot` (the y of its
LOWEST OPAQUE row, where it stands on the floor — not `y` + the PNG's height,
which may end in transparent rows; sort pieces by it to draw them back to front),
`light`, `img` (a transparent PNG as a data URL), `unlit`, and `shadow` {`x`,`y`,`f`}
as its own PNG at its own position, or null where a piece casts none. An isometric room also has `over`: its low front curbs, which go on
top of the pieces. Every image is a `data:image/png;base64,` URL, so decode it rather
than fetching a second file.

tools.name: list_rooms
tools.description:
List your rooms (made with create_room), newest first: id, status, view, name and
doors. get_room(room_id) gives one room's picture, door anchors and walkable rects.

tools.name: delete_room
tools.description:
Permanently delete a room made with create_room. Refused while it (or its furniture's cut)
is being made, and while another of your rooms' saved arrangement uses its pieces. Maps
that placed it keep its picture; objects made from its pieces stay in your objects.

tools.name: cut_out_room_furniture
tools.description:
Cut a painted room's furniture out as movable pieces, each with its own shadow, so it can be
moved, removed or brought into other rooms in the website's room editor — or exported as
separate transparent PNGs, with the furniture-free floor, from the `layers:` JSON get_room
prints when they are ready (see its Download). Only when the user wants to rearrange the
furniture: the painted room is complete without it. Takes ~5-8 minutes; costs 10 generations,
charged when the pieces are ready. Needs Tier 1 (Pixel Apprentice) or higher.

tools.name: search_help

question.description: What you need help with (tools, workflows, billing, features, deployment). Include the context you are working in. Max 2000 characters.

tool.description: A tool's name, e.g. 'animate_character': returns its full reference (every option, price and limit) as written, at once and free. Pass instead of question.

tools.name: agent_feedback
tools.description:
Report something broken, confusing or missing — a PixelLab tool, the sandbox
(build, deploy, git, playtest), the game template code, or the website.
Specific beats polite. Read daily by the team.

tool_name.description: What it's about: a tool, command or file (e.g. 'create_character', 'wrangler deploy', 'src/scenes/Game.ts').

message.description: What you did, what happened, what you expected. Be specific.

area.description: Rough bucket, helps route it: generation (art tools), chat_tool, template (the game template's code), sandbox (build, deploy, git, playtest), website, other.

tools.name: create_tiles_pro
tools.description:
Create pixel art tiles (pro): up to 16 independent tiles of one shape per
call. Returns a tile id at once; poll get_tiles_pro(tile_id) (~1-2 min).
Needs a tier 1 subscription or higher.

- Shape mode (default): tile_type, tile_size, tile_view; number each tile.
- Style mode: style_images sets style and size; shape controls are ignored.
- tile_feature="tileset": a connectable terrain transition ("grass to water"),
  16 corner tiles or a 32-tile hex coastline; oblique exists only as this.
- palette + palette_name: every pixel is one of your hex colours.

Other tools: square top-down terrain transitions -> create_topdown_tileset
(transition width, per-terrain references, style matching); paths ->
create_path_tiles; walls, floors and oblique buildings -> create_building_kit.

Cost: priced by the sheet, 16 cells of the tile AS DRAWN, so tile_view,
tile_view_angle, tile_depth_ratio and tile_height move it as well as tile_size.
Independent tiles: 10 generations while that sheet stays small, else 15; they
never reach 25 (for every type but oblique: 16-48px 10, 64px 10 or 15 by view,
larger mostly 15; oblique extrudes side faces, 15 from 64px). Tilesets reach
15 or 25 at 96px and above. The sheet holds 16 tiles up to 64px for every type
but oblique; above that take get_tiles_pro's count rather than planning on 16.

Full reference (cost by size and view, map rules, every parameter):
search_help(tool="create_tiles_pro").

description.description: Number each tile: '1). grass tile 2). stone tile 3). lava tile'. At most 16 independent tiles per call: split a longer list. A tileset: the transition, e.g. 'grass to water'.

tile_type.description: hex flat-top, hex_pointy pointy-top, isometric diamond, octagon, square_topdown square at an angle. oblique (square top, depth extruded down-right) needs tile_feature='tileset'.

tile_size.description: Tile size in px; 32 is recommended.

tile_height.description: Non-square tiles, e.g. 128 for 64x128. Maps take groups made without tile_height (or with tile_size or 2x it): for a flat 2:1 iso floor omit it and set tile_view_angle=30 and tile_depth_ratio=0.

tile_view.description: Depth: top-down none, high ~15%, low ~30%, side ~50%. Map rows step tile_size x sin(angle) (64px tiles at low top-down -> 22px rows), so flat orthographic ground drawn this way overlaps: use top-down.

tile_view_angle.description: Degrees, overrides tile_view: 0 side, 90 top-down; isometric 30 is 2:1.

tile_flat_top_px.description: Isometric only: top/bottom cap width, 2 classic or 4 modern.

style_images.description: Tiles to copy style and size from; shape controls are then ignored. Each {"image": "<reference>"} (URL, upload:, gallery:, job: or pixel tool id) or inline {"base64", "width", "height"}.

style_options.description: What to copy from style_images, as JSON: {"color_palette": true, "outline": true, "detail": true, "shading": true}

outline_mode.description: "outline": grey shading with outlines. "segmentation": red/blue zones, no outlines, cleaner tiles.

oblique_lean.description: Oblique tilesets: shear per pixel of depth, 0.5 cabinet, 1 = 45 degrees (default).

boundary_amplitude.description: tile_feature='tileset' only (square_topdown, isometric, oblique, hex, hex_pointy). Uneven boundary: how far the terrain border meanders instead of a straight edge, 0 = straight (default) to 0.3. Tiles still connect seamlessly.

boundary_seed.description: Boundary shape for boundary_amplitude (the website's Reshuffle): another number gives a different coastline at the same amount.

elevation.description: tile_feature='tileset' on square_topdown, isometric or oblique only. Terrain height in pixels: raises the first terrain into a plateau with a cliff face down to the second. 0 = flat (default), at most 12; the cap is what fits the tile's top face and wall at this size and view, and a larger value is refused with it.

step_slope.description: Edge steepness, with elevation above 0: how far the drop spreads sideways. 0 = a cliff straight down (default), up to 2 = a gentle slope over more ground (the website steps it by 0.25).

palette.description: Target palette, 2 to 256 hex colours as a JSON array, e.g. ["#081820", "#346856", "#88c070", "#e0f8d0"] for Game Boy or ["#000000", "#ffffff"] for 1-bit. Every pixel the tool draws is one of them; pixels you supplied (a direction you drew) stay as they are.

tools.name: create_path_tiles
tools.description:
Create a connectable PATH/ROAD tile set (18 configs).

Generates straights, corners, T-junctions, a crossroads, dead-ends and a
plain ground tile, all sharing one look. The set ships per-tile edge rules
(N/E/S/W bitmasks), so a map editor or your own autotiler can pick the right
piece from a cell's painted neighbours — see get_tiles_pro for the rules.

For terrain transitions (grass meeting water) use
create_tiles_pro(tile_feature="tileset"); for walls and floors use
create_building_kit.

For a console or palette look (1-bit, Game Boy, PICO-8, any palette from Lospec)
pass `palette` as its hex colours plus `palette_name`: the set is drawn for them
and every pixel of every tile is one of them.

Cost: 10-25 generations, set by the SHEET its road set is drawn on — and that
set is never shrunk to reach a cheaper canvas the way create_tiles_pro's
independent tiles are, so tile_view_angle moves the price as much as tile_size.
A square_topdown set only takes tile_size=32, where the default angle prices it
at 15, tile_view_angle=90 (straight down, so the cells are at their tallest) at
25, and a near-side angle at 10. isometric takes 48-96: 48px is 10 at any
angle, 64px is 10 (15 at 90), and 96px is 25 unless the angle is near-side.
Flatter art is the cheaper art here.

Non-blocking: returns a tile id immediately; poll with get_tiles_pro.

description.description: Ground and path, e.g. "grass with a dirt road" or "stone floor with a mosaic walkway". Describe both — the set renders the path over the ground.

tile_type.description: Tile shape. square_topdown: square tiles at an angle. isometric: diamond/rhombus.

tile_size.description: Tile size in pixels. square_topdown requires exactly 32; isometric accepts 48-96.

tile_view_angle.description: Camera elevation in degrees (0=side, 90=straight down). Isometric 30 is 2:1 isometric; 26 and 27 are drawn and saved as 30.

tile_depth_ratio.description: Tile thickness as a fraction of tile size.

outline_mode.description: "outline" = gray shading with outlines. "segmentation" = color zones, cleaner seamless edges.

On the three tools that have a standard mode — create_character, create_topdown_tileset, animate_object — ANY palette setting needs mode='pro': standard refuses palette and max_colors, alone or together. Every other tool taking them has no standard mode and accepts them always.

tools.name: create_building_kit
tools.description:
Create a BUILDING KIT — floor, connectable walls, doorways, pillar, stairs.

Generates a matched vocabulary of architectural pieces (walls 1-3 tiles
high) you assemble into structures. Wall segments carry outline rules so a
cell's walls follow the shape of the floor area you place them around.

Roofs: the kit has two. The upper-floor tile (floor_roof, floor2's material)
is FLAT — lay it on top of the walls for a flat roof, terrace or upper
storey. The roof pieces (materials layout only) slope up from every eave
(`roof_profile`) and flatten inside. A description such as "flat roof"
changes the material only, never this shape.

Cost: `layout` moves the price more than anything else. layout='materials'
is 10 generations at every type and every tile_size, because the swatches it
paints fit a small sheet whatever the pieces end up looking like.
layout='grid' paints each piece on its own, so its sheet grows with the tile,
and how fast depends on the projection: isometric and square_topdown are 10 at
32px, 15 at 48px and 25 from 64px up, while oblique's flatter cells stay 10
through 48px and reach only 15 at 64px. isometric DEFAULTS to grid while
square_topdown and oblique default to materials — so the common isometric kit
at tile_size=64 is 25 generations, the dearest call in the family, and the same
kit with layout='materials' is 10. wall_tiles only matters where it tips a
sheet over a band: an isometric 64px grid kit is 15 with wall_tiles=1 and 25
with 2 or 3.
The call asks you to have 15 free, which is a reserve rather than the price:
keep 25 free for an isometric grid kit above 48px, or it is refused after
the reserve passes.

Not a terrain set: for grass-meets-water use
create_tiles_pro(tile_feature="tileset"); for roads use create_path_tiles.

For a console or palette look (1-bit, Game Boy, PICO-8, any palette from Lospec)
pass `palette` as its hex colours plus `palette_name`: the kit is drawn for them
and every pixel of every piece is one of them.

Non-blocking: returns a tile id immediately; poll with get_tiles_pro.

wall_description.description: Wall material, e.g. "stone brick walls" or "weathered timber walls".

floor_description.description: Floor material, e.g. "wooden plank floor" or "flagstone floor".

tile_type.description: Projection. isometric: diamond lattice. square_topdown: plain square grid. oblique: true square top with walls sheared down-right at 45 degrees.

tile_size.description: Tile size in pixels. isometric requires 32-96; square_topdown and oblique accept 16-96.

floor2_description.description: Upper-storey / roof surface material: paints the flat upper-floor tile (floor_roof) and the roof pieces. Defaults to the wall material. It sets the material only, not the roof's shape — see roof_profile.

roof_profile.description: Shape of a building kit's roof pieces' edges (materials layout only): gable = straight slope, round = curved. Each edge rises over half a tile and the roof is flat inside, so only a one-tile-wide roof peaks. There is no flat roof piece; for a flat roof or a roof terrace, lay the upper-floor tile (floor_roof) on top of the walls. Default gable.

layout.description: grid: each shaped piece is painted individually (richer; isometric default). materials: flat swatches are painted and pieces rendered from them (more consistent; default for square_topdown/oblique).

wall_angle.description: square_topdown only: wall storey height as its own camera angle, decoupled from the ground pitch.

oblique_lean.description: Wall shear per pixel of height. 0.5 = classic cabinet (~27 degrees), 1.0 = a full 45 degree diagonal.

tile_view_angle.description: Camera elevation in degrees. Isometric 30 is 2:1 isometric, which is also what you get when it's left out; 26 and 27 are drawn and saved as 30.

outline_mode.description: "outline" = gray shading with outlines. "segmentation" = color zones, cleaner seamless edges.

tools.name: get_tiles_pro
tools.description: Get tiles pro by ID. Returns tile data and storage URLs if completed, or progress if processing.

tile_id.description: The UUID of the tiles pro to retrieve. Each returned tile carries the placement rule its sheet uses; the bit meanings are edge/4: bit0=N bit1=E bit2=S bit3=W; a set bit means the painted feature continues across that edge; edge/6: 6 hex edges CCW from vertex 0; a set bit means the OTHER terrain (water) lies beyond that edge; corner/4: NW<<3 | NE<<2 | SW<<1 | SE; a set bit means the first terrain occupies that corner.

tools.name: list_tiles_pro
tools.description:
List your tiles (pro). One line per tile with status.
Use get_tiles_pro(tile_id) for full details.

limit.description: Maximum number of tiles to return

tools.name: delete_tiles_pro
tools.description:
Delete tiles pro by ID. Only the owner can delete their own tiles.

This action is permanent and cannot be undone.

tile_id.description: The UUID of the tiles pro to delete

tools.name: import_tiles
tools.description:
Import your own tiles or tileset sheet (free) — what the website's Import does.

Nothing is generated and nothing is charged. kind='tiles' makes a tile group from
one image per tile (as create_tiles_pro's groups: get_tiles_pro, maps). A tileset
kind cuts one PixelLab-layout sheet into its 16 (or 25) Wang tiles with new base
tile ids, so it chains, maps and downloads like a generated tileset. Sizes are
checked, and a refusal names the size needed.

kind.description: What to make. tiles: a tile group (get_tiles_pro), one image per tile. topdown_tileset / sidescroller_tileset: a Wang tileset (get_topdown_tileset / get_sidescroller_tileset) from ONE sheet.

images.description: JSON array of image references: an https URL, upload:<id>, gallery:<id>, job:<id>[:<index>], a data URL or base64 PNG. kind='tiles': one per tile, 1-32. A tileset kind: exactly one sheet in PixelLab's layout - the 15-tileset sheet a tileset download gives (4x4 tiles, 4x8 for a tall set) or the 8-wide native sheet.

tile_size.description: kind='tiles': required, the tile size in pixels (the images' width; square_topdown and octagon tiles are tile_size square). Tilesets: 16, 24, 32 or 64, read from the sheet when omitted; give it when a size reads two ways (256x256 is a 64px 4x4 or a 32px 8-wide sheet).

description.description: kind='tiles': what the tiles are (default 'Imported tiles').

tile_view.description: kind='tiles': the view they are drawn in (default low top-down).

tile_view_angle.description: kind='tiles': view angle in degrees, if known.

lower_description.description: Tilesets: the lower terrain (sidescroller: the platform).

transition_description.description: Tilesets: the strip between the terrains.

name.description: Tilesets: display name (default: cropped from the descriptions).

tools.name: create_portrait_character
tools.description:
Convert between a portrait and a character sprite (pro).

Preserves the subject's identity/outfit while matching an internal
size-specific pixel-art style for the chosen view. For a fixed palette
(Game Boy, PICO-8, any palette from Lospec) pass `palette` as its hex colours:
the sprite is drawn for them and every pixel is one of them.

This tool starts asynchronous generation that returns immediately with a job
ID. Use get_portrait_character to check status and retrieve the sprite.

Examples:
- Turn a character portrait into a top-down RPG sprite:
  create_portrait_character(image_url=<portrait_png_url>, direction="portrait_to_character", view="low top-down", result_size=64)
- Turn a full-body sprite into a bust portrait:
  create_portrait_character(image_url=<character_png_url>, direction="character_to_portrait", view="low top-down", result_size=64)

Generation time: ~30-80 seconds (async processing)

image.description: Input image as base64-encoded PNG. PREFER image_url because MCP/LLM clients can alter or truncate opaque base64 tool arguments.

image_url.description: Public https, data: or `upload:<id>` URL for the input image. Prefer this over image so the original bytes do not pass through the model.

direction.description: portrait_to_character: portrait in → full-body character sprite out. character_to_portrait: character in → bust portrait out.

view.description: Camera angle. low top-down: classic 3/4 RPG. high top-down: steeper. side: eye-level sidescroller.

result_size.description: Output sprite size in pixels. Cost: 16/32/48/64 = 10 generations; 128/160 are drawn with extra detail = 15 generations.

palette.description: Target palette, 2 to 256 hex colours as a JSON array, e.g. ["#081820", "#346856", "#88c070", "#e0f8d0"] for Game Boy or ["#000000", "#ffffff"] for 1-bit. Every pixel the tool draws is one of them; pixels you supplied (a direction you drew) stay as they are.

palette_name.description: Optional name of the palette (e.g. 'Game Boy', 'PICO-8'); naming it helps the look. It only LABELS the colours you pass in palette rather than looking any up, so it cannot be sent on its own.

max_colors.description: At most this many colours (2-64). With a palette, they are picked from it. On the three tools that have a standard mode — create_character, create_topdown_tileset, animate_object — ANY palette setting needs mode='pro': standard refuses palette and max_colors, alone or together. Every other tool taking them has no standard mode and accepts them always.

tools.name: get_portrait_character
tools.description:
Get a portrait ↔ character result by job id.

Returns the sprite (inline + download URL) if completed, or progress/error.

job_id.description: The job id returned by create_portrait_character.

tools.name: set_character_portrait
tools.description:
Attach a bust portrait to a character, or remove the portrait or one of its
talking expressions (no generation, free).

A portrait is the starting frame for talking animations — set one, then
create_vocal_animation generates the mouth positions from it. Overwrites any
existing portrait. Pass exactly one of image, from_job_id, remove_portrait or
remove_expression.

Examples:
- Straight from a portrait job:
  set_character_portrait("<character-uuid>", from_job_id="<portrait-job-uuid>")
- From your own artwork:
  set_character_portrait("<character-uuid>", image=<png_base64>)
- Delete the portrait:
  set_character_portrait("<character-uuid>", remove_portrait=True)
- Delete the angry expression, keep the rest:
  set_character_portrait("<character-uuid>", remove_expression="angry")

character_id.description: Character whose portrait (or expression) to set or remove.

image.description: Portrait as base64-encoded PNG. Square is ideal; a non-square image is centred on a transparent square canvas.

from_job_id.description: Instead of `image`: the job id of a completed create_portrait_character run. The sprite is copied straight across, so it never has to pass through your context.

remove_portrait.description: Delete the character's portrait instead of setting one. Expressions already made from it stay and keep working with create_talking_gif and get_lip_sync; a new expression needs a portrait again.

remove_expression.description: Delete this one expression (mood) from the character's mouth positions instead. The others stay, and the rows below it in the spritesheet move up; removing the last one removes the whole set. Make it again with create_vocal_animation.

tools.name: create_vocal_animation
tools.description:
Generate a talking mouth-position set ("visemes") for a character's portrait.

Produces one keyframe per mouth shape, all sharing the chosen expression, so
the character can be lip-synced to any line of text afterwards. Building the
set costs generations ONCE; turning it into talking animations with
create_talking_gif is free.

Works two ways. With `character_id` the set is saved onto that character, so
every later call needs only the id — use this when the character exists.
With `image` you generate straight from a portrait and nothing is stored; the
frames live in the job for 8 hours and you reference it by job id.

Cost: 3 generations for the default 7 mouth positions on a portrait up to
64px. Two things scale it — the position count sets how many drawing passes
run (2 passes for 3 positions, 3 for 5 or 7, 4 for 12) and the portrait's size
sets what one pass costs (1 generation up to 64px, 2 at 96-128px, 4 at 160px,
5 at 192px, 8 at 256px). So 7 positions is 3 at 64px, 6 at 128px and 24 at
256px, while 12 positions on a 64px portrait is 4. engine="pixminimax" prices
a pass at 1 generation at every size, so a big portrait is far cheaper there.
A set can need a few extra passes to fill in a position, so the figure in the
submit receipt is the one to quote; those extra passes stop once a call
reaches 40 generations, which is the ceiling for any size and count. Turning
the set into talking animations with create_talking_gif is free, however many
lines you lip-sync.

Requires a subscription (or trial). The character form needs a portrait set
first. To delete an expression again:
set_character_portrait(character_id, remove_expression="angry").

Examples:
- Default talking set for a character:
  create_vocal_animation(character_id="<uuid>")
- Add an angry expression to the same character:
  create_vocal_animation(character_id="<uuid>", mood="angry")
- Just a portrait, no character:
  create_vocal_animation(image=<portrait_png>)

Generation time: ~2-5 minutes (async processing)

character_id.description: Character to generate the expression for; it must already have a portrait, and the finished set is saved onto it so later calls only need the character id. Mutually exclusive with `image`.

image.description: Generate from this portrait PNG (base64) instead, without a character. Nothing is stored: the mouth positions come back from get_vocal_animation and you pass that job id to create_talking_gif. Use this when the user only has a portrait. Mutually exclusive with `character_id`. Max 256x256.

mood.description: Expression baked into the face (brows/eyes/cheeks). The mouth shapes are the same across moods. One call per mood; each is stored as its own row of the character's vocal grid.

viseme_count.description: How many mouth positions to generate. 3 = minimal (tiny portraits), 5 = basic, 7 = recommended, 12 = high quality (large close-ups). Must match across moods for the same character.

no_background.description: Cut out the background so frames are transparent PNGs — usually what you want for compositing over a game scene.

engine.description: Which generator draws the mouth positions. 'v3' (default) is the original one. 'pixminimax' (PixMiniMax, beta) keeps the eyes, brows and head still while only the mouth moves, and costs the same at every portrait size up to 256px: 3 generations for 7 positions (2 for 3, 4 for 12), where v3 costs 3 at 64px, 6 at 128px and 24 at 256px.

tools.name: get_vocal_animation
tools.description:
Check a vocal-animation job and see which mouth positions have landed.

Mouth positions stream in as they are picked, so a running job already
reports partial progress. On completion the set is saved onto the character
and ready for create_talking_gif.

job_id.description: The job id returned by create_vocal_animation.

tools.name: create_talking_gif
tools.description:
Turn text into a talking GIF using a character's existing mouth positions.

FREE — no generations are spent. This only sequences frames that
create_vocal_animation already produced, so the expensive step happens once
per expression and every line of dialogue after that costs nothing.

Examples:
- create_talking_gif(character_id="<uuid>", text_to_speak="Welcome, traveller!")
- create_talking_gif(character_id="<uuid>", text_to_speak="You dare return?!", mood="angry")
- portrait-only, no character:
  create_talking_gif(from_job_id="<vocal job id>", text_to_speak="Hello!")

Returns immediately (no job to poll).

text_to_speak.description: The line of dialogue to lip-sync. Mouth shapes are derived from the letters, so any language using the latin alphabet works.

character_id.description: Character with a vocal animation. Mutually exclusive with `from_job_id`.

from_job_id.description: Use a portrait-only set instead: the job id from create_vocal_animation(image=...). Mutually exclusive with `character_id`. Available for 8 hours after that job finished.

mood.description: Which generated expression to talk with. Defaults to the character's first available expression.

frame_ms.description: Milliseconds per mouth position (~90ms reads as natural speech; raise it for a slower delivery). GIF stores delays in 10ms steps, so this is rounded to the nearest 10 and the response reports what was actually used.

hold_ms.description: Pause on the closed mouth at the end so a looping GIF has a beat between takes.

tools.name: get_lip_sync
tools.description:
Get the lip-sync frame plan for a line of dialogue — for animating in a game.

FREE, and nothing is rendered. Use this instead of create_talking_gif when the
game should animate the mouth itself: you get the spritesheet URL, the row for
the expression, and a frame list giving the column to draw and how long to hold
it. create_talking_gif is the better answer when you just want a playable file.

Timings are exact here — unlike a GIF, an engine can hold a frame for any
duration.

Example:
- get_lip_sync("<uuid>", "Welcome to the village, traveller!")

Returns immediately (no job to poll).

character_id.description: Character with a vocal animation (see create_vocal_animation). This tool is character-only on purpose: it hands the engine a spritesheet URL to load, and a portrait-only set has no stored spritesheet — for that case use create_talking_gif(from_job_id=...) instead.

text_to_speak.description: The line of dialogue to lip-sync.

mood.description: Which generated expression to use. Defaults to the character's first available expression.

frame_ms.description: Milliseconds to hold each mouth position.

hold_ms.description: Extra time on the final closed mouth.

tools.name: create_font
tools.description:
Create a pixel-art font (pro).

Produces a glyph atlas + a ready-to-use TrueType (.ttf) font with uppercase,
lowercase, digits 0-9, and common game-UI punctuation. Costs 15 generations
or at least $0.115 in credits.

This tool starts asynchronous generation that returns immediately with a job
ID. Use get_font to check status and retrieve the atlas + font.

Example:
  create_font(description="warm orange arcade font", weight="Bold", glyph_px=16)

Generation time: ~30-80 seconds (async processing)

description.description: Style description of the font, e.g. 'warm orange arcade font'.

glyph_px.description: Native glyph resolution in pixels (real bitmap size per glyph). The atlas is a 10x8 grid of 80 glyphs, ROW-MAJOR, so cell i holds the i-th character of "ABCDEFGHIJKLMNOPQRSTUVWXYZabcdefghijklmnopqrstuvwxyz.,!?:;'"-+()0123456789/%*=_$" — slice it with that order. There is no space glyph.

font_name.description: Explicit font family name; defaults to '{description} {weight}'.

tools.name: create_music
tools.description:
Make music for your game: two takes of a song from a description of its style.

Instrumental by default; with vocals, send lyrics or set auto_lyrics. Both takes
are saved to your library on the website, where they can go in your games.
restyle_song_id plays one of your songs again in a new style. For music that
repeats seamlessly, call make_music_loop on a finished instrumental take.

Cost: 10 generations, or $0.08 in credits, for the two takes; charged once they
are made. Needs a tier 2 subscription or higher.

Generation time: ~20-60 seconds, up to 2.5 minutes when busy (async). Poll with
get_music or wait_for_jobs; the result is an audio link (MP3).

Example: create_music(style="Upbeat 8-bit dungeon theme: a fast square-wave lead,
a pulsing triangle bass and crisp noise drums, ending on a sting.", bpm=140)

style.description: What the music sounds like, in a sentence or two that gives each instrument a role, plus the mood and how it ends: 'Calm chiptune town theme: a soft square-wave melody over a bouncy bass, light noise drums, ending on a held chord.' A list of tags comes out flat; artist names are refused. Put sounds to keep out in exclude, not as 'no ...' here. improve_music_style writes a short idea out in full.

instrumental.description: true: no vocals (game music). false: a song with vocals, which needs lyrics or auto_lyrics.

lyrics.description: With vocals: the words to sing, one line per line, with section tags on their own lines: [Intro], [Verse], [Pre-Chorus], [Chorus], [Bridge], [Instrumental Break], [Outro], [End]. A tag can carry one direction: [Chorus: full band, doubled vocals]. write_music_lyrics drafts some.

auto_lyrics.description: With vocals: have the lyrics written for the song instead of sending them (send no lyrics, length_s or style_weight). get_music shows what it sings once it is made.

about.description: With auto_lyrics: what the song is about; may be empty.

length_s.description: Length to aim for, 10-360 s. Default: auto, fitted to the song (a new style: the song's own length).

bpm.description: Tempo, 60-180 BPM, added to the style. Default: auto.

voice.description: With vocals: the voice, added to the style, e.g. 'warm female voice', 'bright female voice', 'breathy female voice', 'powerful female voice'. Ignored for instrumentals.

exclude.description: Sounds to keep out, short phrases: 'fade out, electric guitar'. An instrumental keeps out 'vocals, singing' without being asked.

style_weight.description: How closely to follow the style, 0-1. Default: 0.5.

name.description: The song's name in the library. Default: the style's first words. The second take gets ' (take 2)'.

restyle_song_id.description: Make one of your songs again in this new style: the same melody, its vocals and lyrics kept (send no lyrics, auto_lyrics or about).

project_id.description: Internal Game Builder project context; the finished song is linked after generation.

tools.name: make_music_loop
tools.description:
Make one of your songs into game music that loops seamlessly.

The song is made again so that the part between its intro and its ending
repeats without a seam: two new takes, each with loop points. Play the take to
loop_end, then jump back to loop_start (get_music shows both, in seconds). The
intro plays once, the ending never. Instrumental songs only, for now.

tools.name: create_image_pixflux
tools.description:
Generate a freeform pixel-art image from text (no character/object rig).

Use this for anything that is just an image: item icons, backgrounds, card

for an asset-pack prop use create_1_direction_object; for a map prop that
matches an existing map's style use create_map_object.

Canvas is 16-400px per side, total area 32x32 to 400x400.

Examples:
- create_image_pixflux(description="health potion bottle", width=64, height=64, no_background=True)
- create_image_pixflux(description="forest background", width=320, height=180)
- img2img over your own sprite:
  create_image_pixflux(description="same knight but in gold armor", init_image_base64=<png>, init_image_strength=150)

init_image_strength is how much of the input is KEPT (inverted vs most
img2img APIs): 500 barely moves it, 300 is subtle, ~150 is a visible edit,
~50 keeps only the rough composition. For editing an image use edit_image;
for fixing one region use inpaint_image.

Cost: 1 generation. Generation time: ~10-40 seconds (async).
Poll with get_image(job_id).

description.description: What to draw (e.g. 'cute dragon', 'health potion bottle').

width.description: Canvas width in pixels. Defaults to the init_image width, or 128 when there is no init_image. The 16px floor is per-axis: the TOTAL area must still be at least 32x32=1024px, so 16x16 is rejected while 16x64 is fine. This area floor is THIS tool's; for a 16x16 or 20x20 icon use create_image_pixen, whose floor is per side (the legal small canvases are the squares 16, 20, 24 and 28), at the same 1 generation.

height.description: Canvas height in pixels. Defaults to the init_image height, or 128 when there is no init_image. See width for the area rule.

no_background.description: Remove the background: True for sprites/items, False for scenes. Unset follows init_image, else False. direction.description: Which way the subject faces (weakly guiding).

text_guidance_scale.description: How literally to follow the description. Higher = more literal.

init_image_base64.description: Base64 PNG to start from (img2img). Must be exactly width x height — omit width/height to adopt its size.

init_image_url.description: Alternative to init_image_base64: an https, data: or `upload:<id>` URL to the init PNG. PREFER THIS for anything but a tiny sprite. Give one, not both.

init_image_strength.description: How much of init_image is PRESERVED — the opposite of the usual img2img 'strength'. Higher = closer to the input: 500 barely changes it, 300 is subtle, 150 (default) is a real edit, ~50 keeps only the composition.

tools.name: create_image_pixen
tools.description:
Generate a freeform pixel-art image with the Pixen model.

Pixen is the newer of the two fast generators and holds up better on small
sprites. Pick between the three text-to-image tools like this:
- create_image_pixflux — when you need an init image (img2img), a palette
  given as an image, isometric, or shading control.
- create_image_pixen — this one; cleaner small sprites, bigger canvas.
- create_image_pro — best quality, returns a set of candidates, costs more;
  takes a palette as hex colours (1-bit, Game Boy, PICO-8, NES, Lospec).

Canvas: 16-768 per side and each side must be a multiple of 4; total area
16x16 to 512x512. Below 32 the canvas must be SQUARE, so the small sizes
are 16x16, 20x20, 24x24 and 28x28.

Cost: 1 generation. Generation time: ~10-40 seconds (async).
Poll with get_image(job_id).

description.description: What to draw (e.g. 'ornate iron key', 'mossy stone wall').

width.description: Canvas width in pixels. Must be a multiple of 4; width must equal height when either side is below 32. What the two sides are held to together is an AREA of 262,144 px, NOT a 512 px side: neither side has to be 512 or under and the canvas need not be square, so a 640x360 background (230,400 px) and 768x340 are both fine at 1 generation, while 768x384 (294,912 px) is over. 512x512 is only what that area looks like square.

height.description: Canvas height in pixels. Must be a multiple of 4; height must equal width when either side is below 32.

no_background.description: Return the subject on a transparent background. True for sprites and items, False for scenes. Up to 256x256 of area (65,536 px, e.g. 256x256 or 512x128); larger canvases are refused with it on.

direction.description: Which way the subject faces (weakly guiding).

project_id.description: Internal Game Builder project context; the finished image is linked after generation.

tools.name: create_image_pro
tools.description:
Create Image (Pro): best-quality pixel art, and one call returns a SET of
candidates, not one image -- how many is the canvas's band in the Cost ladder
below. Takes up to 4 labelled reference_images, a style
image, and a palette as hex colours (1-bit, Game Boy, PICO-8, NES, Lospec).

Siblings: create_image_pixflux for img2img, isometric or shading control;
create_image_pixen for clean small sprites at 1 generation;
create_image_pro_flash for ONE image at 5-9 generations. This one when quality
matters more than cost. No facing control: to turn a picture into 8 facings use
create_object_pro_flash(first_frame_base64=..., n_directions=8).

Generation time: ~1-10 minutes (async). Poll with get_image(job_id).

Cost: 10, 15 or 25 generations for the CALL, never per candidate, so a small
canvas buys more tries, not a discount. Price and candidate count are one
ascending ladder of contiguous bands -- find your own size and read that
band's two numbers, because the price does NOT rise with size and a
neighbouring band carries different ones. `size px: generations, candidates`
= 16-32: 10, 64 | 33-35: 15, 49 | 36-41: 15, 36 | 42-42: 15, 25 |
43-50: 10, 25 | 51-64: 10, 16 | 65-84: 15, 9 | 85-85: 15, 16 |
86-128: 10, 4 | 129-170: 15, 4 | 171-256: 10, 1 | 257-341: 15, 1 |
342-512: 25, 1. So 40x40 is 15 generations and 36 candidates while 48x48 is
10 and 25, and 192x192 is 10 and a single candidate where 160x160 is 15 and
4. A non-square canvas reads both sides, not the longer one: the submit
receipt's `cost: N generations` is exact, and a cancel after submitting
usually still pays for it.

Full reference (non-square prices, canvas maxima, references, style, palette):
search_help(tool="create_image_pro").

description.description: What to draw (e.g. 'ornate iron key with a ruby inlay').

width.description: Canvas width. The cap is an area of about a quarter megapixel by nearest aspect ratio: 512x512 square, 688x384 at 16:9, 792x336 the widest. Larger is refused before queueing.

height.description: Canvas height. Max depends on aspect ratio (see width).

no_background.description: Transparent background (the default, for assets). False for scenes and backdrops.

reference_images.description: Up to 4 labelled images, a JSON array of {"url" (preferred) or "base64", "usage"}, e.g. [{"url": "https://...", "usage": "outfit and armour"}]. "usage" says what to take from each. A "url" may be https, data: or an `upload:<id>` from get_upload_url.

style_image_base64.description: An image whose art style (palette, outline, detail, shading) the result matches; style_copy narrows which.

style_image_url.description: https, data: or `upload:<id>` URL instead of style_image_base64; prefer it. Give one, not both.

style_copy.description: Any of color_palette, outline, detail, shading to take from the style image (needs one). Default all four; with a palette, all but color_palette, which is then refused.

palette.description: 2 to 256 hex colours, e.g. ["#081820", "#346856", "#88c070", "#e0f8d0"] for Game Boy; every pixel of the result is one of them.

palette_name.description: Names the palette, e.g. 'Game Boy'; helps the look. Needs palette.
