tools.name: edit_image
tools.description:
Edit an existing image with a text instruction or a reference image (pro).

This returns YOUR image, edited — the pose, composition and pixel style are
preserved and only what you asked for changes. Use it to recolour armour, add
an accessory, change an expression, or restyle frames to match a reference.

Two modes, picked by what you pass:
- text edit: edit_image(images_base64=[<png>], description="give him a red cape")
- reference edit: edit_image(images_base64=[<png>], reference_image_base64=<png>)

Which edit tool:
- one image, or the same edit on separate images (a character's directions):
  edit_image (this; edit_image_pixen is cheaper for a single sprite)
- an animation's frames, changed by a text instruction: edit_animation
- an animation's frames, re-dressed from a reference image: transfer_outfit
Reference mode here is for one image.

Related tools: create_image_pixflux(init_image_base64=...) regenerates the whole image
instead of editing it; create_map_object generates a NEW object matching a
map's style and returns a cutout, not your edited image.

Frame limit depends on output size: <=64px 16 frames, <=80px 9, <=128px 4,
larger 1 (one fewer in reference mode). Inputs max 512x512.

Cost: 10 generations for any output canvas up to 256x256, 15 up to 341x341,
25 above — so 64x64, 128x128 and 256x256 all cost the same 10, and the frame
grid is already priced in: a single 64x64 edit costs the same as sixteen of
them, so batch your frames where they fit. A non-square canvas is measured at
its own aspect ratio and can land a band lower than its longer side suggests.
HOW MANY frames fit is a separate ladder from the price and shares none of
its steps: 16 frames up to 64px, 9 up to 80px, 4 up to 128px, and a single
frame at any larger size (one fewer in reference mode, where the reference
takes a cell). So sixteen 64x64 frames are one call at 10, while 263 icons at
144x144 are 263 calls at 10 each — batching pays only up to 128px, and above
it the price per call is unchanged.
Generation time: ~30-90 seconds (async). Poll with get_image(job_id).

images_base64.description: Base64 PNG(s) to edit — pass a one-element list for a single image. Several frames get the SAME edit applied consistently (useful for animation frames or a character's directions). Max 512x512 each. PREFER image_urls — MCP clients routinely truncate large inline base64.

image_urls.description: Alternative to images_base64: https, data: or `upload:<id>` (POST /v2/uploads with this same bearer token) URLs to the PNG(s) to edit, in the same one-per-frame list form. PREFER THIS for anything but tiny sprites. Give urls OR base64, not both.

description.description: What to change (e.g. 'add a red wizard hat', 'make the armor gold'). Required unless reference_image_base64 is given.

reference_image_base64.description: Base64 PNG to copy the appearance of (outfit/colors/details) onto the input image, keeping its pose. Switches the tool into reference mode; description then just refines the instruction. To put an outfit on ANIMATION frames, use transfer_outfit instead.

reference_image_url.description: Alternative to reference_image_base64: an https, data: or `upload:<id>` URL to the reference PNG. PREFER THIS for anything but a tiny sprite. Give one, not both.

width.description: Output width. Defaults to the first input image's width.

height.description: Output height. Defaults to the first input image's height.

no_background.description: Background handling. Default (unset) follows the inputs: if any frame has transparency they all stay transparent, otherwise they stay opaque. Pass False to flatten a transparent input onto white.

project_id.description: Internal Game Builder project context; the finished image is linked after generation.

tools.name: edit_image_pixen
tools.description:
Edit an image with a text instruction on the Pixen model (fast, 1 generation).

Returns YOUR image edited — pose, composition and pixel style are preserved
and only what you asked for changes.

Pick between the two edit tools:
- edit_image_pixen — this one; 1 generation, ~10-40s, ONE frame, input max
  256px per side and output max 256x256 in AREA. The default for a single
  sprite.
- edit_image — pro quality, 10-25 generations, ~30-90s, edits up to 16
  frames consistently in one call, accepts a reference image and inputs up
  to 512px. Worth it for animation frames, a character's directions, or when
  pixen's result isn't good enough.

Sizes: the input is capped PER SIDE at 256 (crop an oversized source —
never rescale pixel art); the output is capped by AREA at 256x256 =
65,536px, so 128x512 is fine but 320x320 is not. Output defaults to the
input's size. BOTH sides of both must be multiples of 4 — a 63x222 sprite
is rejected; pad it with transparent pixels to 64x224 first (padding keeps
the pixel grid, rescaling destroys it). Need a bigger canvas? edit_image
takes inputs up to 512.

Cost: 1 generation. Generation time: ~10-40 seconds (async).
Poll with get_image(job_id).

description.description: What to change (e.g. 'give him a red cape', 'make the armor gold'). Same 1-500 bound the v2 endpoint enforces — an empty one would queue a job and spend a generation with nothing to edit towards.

image_base64.description: Base64 PNG to edit. Max 256px per side, both sides multiples of 4 (pad with transparent pixels, never rescale). PREFER image_url — MCP clients routinely truncate large inline base64.

image_url.description: Alternative to image_base64: an https, data: or `upload:<id>` URL to the PNG to edit. PREFER THIS for anything but a tiny sprite. Give one, not both.

width.description: Output width, a multiple of 4. Output AREA must be at most 256x256 (65,536px), so 128x512 is fine but 320x320 is not. Defaults to the input image's width. The model re-renders at this size — it does not rescale.

height.description: Output height, a multiple of 4. Defaults to the input image's height.

no_background.description: Background handling. Default (unset) follows the input: a transparent input stays transparent, an opaque one stays opaque.

project_id.description: Internal Game Builder project context; the finished image is linked after generation.

tools.name: create_normal_map
tools.description:
Make the normal map of a sprite or an animation, so a game engine can light it
(Pro 0.5 generation, Lite 0.1 generation).

The map is a PNG the sprite's size: RGB = which way each pixel faces (red right,
green up in the opengl convention, blue toward the viewer), alpha 255 wherever the
sprite shows and 0 elsewhere.
Each part of the sprite gets its own shape — a head is round, a hat a cone, a wall
faces south — so a light moving around it shades it the way a 3D model would.

An animation (`character:<id>:<direction>:<animation>`, a GIF, a strip) comes
back as a strip, one map per frame side by side in frame order, made from one
plan so the light stays steady as it moves.

Use it in Phaser with the Light2D pipeline:
  this.load.image('knight', ['knight.png', 'knight_n.png'])
  sprite.setPipeline('Light2D'); this.lights.enable().setAmbientColor(0x555555)
Godot: assign it as the sprite's normal map (CanvasTexture). Unreal: convention
"directx".

Each slider left out starts where the kind of picture puts it (an isometric box
gets flat faces), which suits most pictures. Lower
surface_detail for clean flat-shaded art, raise part_shapes for a rounder body;
strength makes the whole map stronger or flatter. Cracks, holes and gaps between
plates come out as grooves even when they glow.

mode="lite" (the default, recommended) reads the map from the art alone in about a
second and is almost always as good; mode="pro" plans every part (a head, an arm in
front of the body, a crack sunk in).

Any colours work (painted art too); pixel art gives the cleanest parts.
Cost: Pro 0.5 generation, Lite 0.1 generation — per CALL, not per frame, so a
32-frame strip maps for the same 0.1 as a single sprite and is by far the
cheapest way to light an animation. Charged only when the map is delivered.
One call takes up to 32 frames at 8-512 px a side; a longer animation has to
be split, which costs one charge per call and plans each part separately, so
the lighting can step between them. Time: Pro ~15-60 s, Lite a few seconds
(async). Poll with get_image(job_id).

image.description: The sprite: `character:<id>:<direction>` (a rotation), `character:<id>:<direction>:<animation>` (every frame of that animation), the same for `object:<id>`, `gallery:<id>`, `job:<id>` (an image tool result), `upload:<id>`, a pixelart_workbench result id, an https or data URL of a PNG or GIF, or base64. Prefer a reference or URL to inline base64.

convention.description: opengl: green = up (Godot, Unity, Phaser, most engines); directx: green = down (Unreal).

mode.description: lite (0.1 generation, recommended): from the art alone, in about a second, and almost always as good; set kind with it for isometric, sidescroller and UI art. pro (0.5 generation): each part of the picture is planned, its shape, what is in front, what is sunk into it.

kind.description: What the picture is: character (a character, creature or portrait), object (an item or effect), topdown (a map, scene or tileset seen from above), side (a side view: sidescroller tiles, a landscape), iso (isometric tiles and objects) or ui (panels, buttons, frames). Left out, it is read from the picture; set it when you know, above all for sidescroller, isometric and UI art.

strength.description: How far every pixel tilts away from facing the viewer.

outline_rounding.description: How much the outline rounds off: 0 keeps it flat to the edge.

part_shapes.description: How much the sprite's 3D parts (a round head, an arm's cylinder) add.

surface_detail.description: The art's own light and dark as bumps: chunks bulge, dark lines and cracks sink.

detail_softness.description: How much that detail is blurred, in px: low follows every pixel.

project_id.description: Internal Game Builder project context; the finished image is linked after generation.

tools.name: transfer_outfit
tools.description:
Reskin an existing animation with the outfit from a reference image (pro).

Every frame keeps its pose and motion; only the appearance changes to match
the reference — new armour on a walk cycle, a new colour scheme across an
attack, a weapon carried through the whole sequence.

transfer_outfit(frame_urls=[<f1>, <f2>, ...], reference_image_url=<outfit>)

The reference should be the SAME character in the new outfit. It does not
reliably turn one character into another.

Which edit tool:
- one image, or the same edit on separate images: edit_image
  (edit_image(reference_image_base64=...) copies an outfit onto ONE image)
- an animation's frames, changed by a text instruction: edit_animation
- an animation's frames, re-dressed from a reference image: transfer_outfit
  (this)

Needs 2+ frames. For a stored character's animation pass its frame URLs from
get_character.

Frame limit depends on output size (the reference takes one grid slot):
both sides 32-64px up to 15 frames, both 65-80px up to 8, larger side
81-256px up to 3. Frames over the limit: split across calls with the same
reference and seed.

For a console or palette look (1-bit, Game Boy, PICO-8, any palette from
Lospec) pass `palette` as its hex colours plus `palette_name`: every pixel of
every frame is one of them (the palette, not the reference, sets the colours).

Needs a tier 1 subscription or higher.
Cost: billed by the whole grid, not the frame count — 2 frames cost the same
as 15 at 64x64, so batch them. One ascending ladder by FRAME size, both sides
counting: 32-128 px: 10 | 129-170: 15 | 171-256: 25. So 96x96 and 128x128 are
both 10 while 160x160 is 15 and 200x200 is 25 — these are NOT edit_image's
bands (that tool stays 10 all the way to 256x256), because above 80px the
reference and the frames always share a 2x2 sheet here. Frames per call: 15
up to 64px, 8 up to 80, 3 above, the reference taking one cell.
Generation time: ~1-2 minutes (async).
Poll with get_image(job_id); frames come back in input order.

frames_base64.description: Base64 PNG animation frames to reskin, in order (2 or more). Max 256x256 each. PREFER frame_urls — MCP clients routinely truncate large inline base64.

frame_urls.description: Alternative to frames_base64: https, data: or `upload:<id>` (POST /v2/uploads with this same bearer token) URLs to the frame PNGs, in order. PREFER THIS for anything but tiny sprites. Give urls OR base64, not both.

reference_image_base64.description: Base64 PNG of the SAME character wearing the new outfit (e.g. a re-dressed or recoloured sprite of it). A different character as reference is unreliable — it can freeze the motion or barely change anything. Max 256x256.

reference_image_url.description: Alternative to reference_image_base64: an https, data: or `upload:<id>` URL to the reference PNG. PREFER THIS for anything but a tiny sprite. Give one, not both.

additional_instructions.description: Optional guidance for the transfer, e.g. 'frames show the character from behind' or 'keep the sword in the right hand'.

width.description: Output frame width. Defaults to the widest frame. Frames and reference smaller than this are padded with transparency, centred — never scaled.

height.description: Output frame height. Defaults to the tallest frame.

tools.name: image_to_pixelart
tools.description:
Convert an image, render or photo into pixel art.

This is the general-purpose converter: give it any picture and get pixel art
back at the size you ask for. Use it when a user brings their own artwork,
a screenshot, or an AI render and wants it as a sprite.

Two dials decide how much licence the model takes:
- default (faithful=False, init_image_strength=0) — reinterprets the subject
  as pixel art. Cleanest sprites, least like the original.
- faithful=True with init_image_strength around 100-300 — reproduces the
  source. Use it when the user says "keep it exactly like this". Higher is
  NOT more faithful in a useful way: past ~300 the model stops transforming
  and returns the source image, which is not pixel art.

This is the one converter where YOU pick the output size. When the size does
not matter, image_to_pixelart_pro_flash (6 generations) and
image_to_pixelart_pro (20, tier 1+) redraw more cleanly and pick the size from
the picture.

Related tools: create_portrait_character converts a picture into a character
portrait specifically; unzoom_image is what you want if the input is ALREADY
pixel art that has merely been upscaled — running it through here would
redraw art that only needed downscaling.

Input max area 2048x2048, output max 512x512.

Cost: 1 generation. Generation time: ~20-60 seconds (async).
Poll with get_image(job_id).

image_url.description: Alternative to image_base64: an https, data: or `upload:<id>` URL to the source image. PREFER THIS for anything but a tiny sprite. Give one, not both.

output_width.description: Width of the pixel art result. Defaults to a quarter of the source width. Keep the source's aspect ratio.

output_height.description: Height of the pixel art result. Defaults to a quarter of the source height.

init_image_strength.description: How strongly to start from the source image (img2img). 0 redraws from scratch using the source only as guidance; 100-300 keeps its composition and colors. Do NOT go higher to be 'more faithful' — past ~300 the model barely transforms the input and hands back the source rather than pixel art.

tools.name: unzoom_image
tools.description:
Downscale upscaled pixel art back onto its true pixel grid.

Pixel art found online is almost always scaled up — a 32x32 sprite saved at
512x512, where every art pixel is a 16x16 block. Every tool that takes a
reference or style image works far better on the real 32x32 sprite, and this
recovers it: the pixel grid is detected and the image is downsampled onto it.

Run this FIRST whenever a user supplies pixel art from outside PixelLab and
you are about to pass it to create_image_pixflux(init_image), a style image,
edit_image, or create_character. If the art was never upscaled it is already
at native size and this is unnecessary.

Do not confuse it with image_to_pixelart: that CONVERTS a non-pixel-art
picture, redrawing it. This one only downscales art that is already pixel art.
It always returns some grid: a result with nearly as many colours as pixels
means the input was not upscaled pixel art.

Input must be at least 256x256 (grid detection needs the pixels) and at most
2048x2048 in area.

The result is OPAQUE: transparency is composited onto white. If the user
needs a cut-out sprite, tell them.

Cost: 0.1 generations. Takes a few seconds at most — poll get_image(job_id).

tools.name: reduce_colors
tools.description:
Quantize images onto a smaller, shared palette.

Pixel art reads as pixel art partly because of its restricted palette. AI
output and converted artwork often carry hundreds of near-identical colors;
this snaps them onto a tight palette, optionally with ordered dithering.

Passing several frames in one call is the point: they are quantized TOGETHER,
so an animation or a character's eight directions come back sharing ONE
palette instead of drifting apart frame by frame. Quantizing them one at a
time is the mistake this tool exists to prevent.

Three ways to choose the palette:
- omit num_colors and the palette image — the size is auto-detected
- num_colors — quantize to exactly this many colors
- palette_image — reuse the colors of an existing image (the game's palette)

The result carries a `palette` strip you can feed back as palette_image_base64
to lock later frames onto the same colors.

Total size limit across all frames is 512x512 worth of pixels (sixteen 64x64
frames, or four 128x128).

Cost: 0.1 generations. Runs locally in about a second — poll once with
get_image(job_id).

images_base64.description: Base64 PNG(s) to quantize — pass a one-element list for a single image. All frames must be the same size. PREFER image_urls; MCP clients routinely truncate large inline base64.

image_urls.description: Alternative to images_base64: https, data: or `upload:<id>` (POST /v2/uploads with this same bearer token) URLs to the PNG(s), one per frame. PREFER THIS. Give urls OR base64, not both.

palette_image_base64.description: Base64 PNG whose colors become the palette (max 256 colors) — use it to force frames onto an existing game palette. Cannot be combined with num_colors.

tools.name: animate_image
tools.description:
Animate any image from a text description of the motion.

Works on a loose sprite — unlike animate_character / animate_object, which
need an id of something PixelLab generated.

unchanged, then the generated ones. Play them in order.

256x256 frame allows 8 frames, a 64x64 frame allows all 16.

Cost scales with total pixels (a 64x64 8-frame animation is 1 generation, a
128x128 16-frame one is 4). Generation time: ~30-180 seconds (async).

tools.description:
Animate with text (PixMiniMax): animate any image from a motion description.

Works on a loose sprite — unlike animate_character / animate_object, which
need an id of something PixelLab generated. Same inputs as animate_image;
frame counts are multiples of four, capped by the frame's longer side (see Limits).

get_image returns frame_count + 1 images: index 0 is your input frame
unchanged, then the generated ones. Play them in order.

Examples:
- animate_image_pixminimax(first_frame_url=<png>, description="walking forward", frame_count=8)
- pin the ending: animate_image_pixminimax(first_frame_base64=<open>,
    last_frame_base64=<closed>, description="chest lid closing", frame_count=4)
- short prompt, expanded for you: animate_image_pixminimax(first_frame_url=<png>,
    description="shooting a bow", direction="south", enhance_prompt=True)

Caption fields (subject_description, initial_pose, view, direction) left out
are read off the image by an AI model, which can decline some requests; the
job then fails asking you to send them yourself.

Beta, every plan.
Limits: frame max 256x256; 4 to 40 frames in multiples of 4 at any size.

Cost: priced by generation time, which follows the UPSCALED canvas the model
works on — x4 up to 64px, x2 up to 128px, x1 above (longer side). So 64, 128
and 256 all price identically, and each is the MOST expensive size in its
neighbourhood. At 64/128/256: 4-8 frames = 1 generation, 12-16 = 2, 20-24 = 3,
28 = 4, 32-36 = 5, 40 = 6.
Four pixels over the step is ~3x cheaper on a long clip: 40 frames costs 6 at
128x128 and 2 at 132x132 (likewise 64x64 -> 68x68). Splitting helps too — four
8-frame calls cost 4 where one 32-frame call costs 5.

Powered by MiniMax H3.

tools.name: animate_with_skeleton_v3
tools.description:
Animate with skeleton v3 (beta): animate a sprite along a skeleton you pose, one per frame.

Every frame is drawn from the one reference image, so the character keeps its
identity while the pose is exactly what you send. Use this when you hold a rig
or can derive skeletons; for a stored PixelLab character, animate_character
with a template animation is far less work.
Nothing returns a template clip's keypoints to an API caller, so there is no
library of walk cycles to fetch: derive them from your sprite with
estimate_skeleton (it returns this tool's exact keypoint shape), bring your own
rig (COCO-18 maps straight across, see `keypoints`), or use
animate_character(mode="skeleton-v3"), which poses a template clip onto a
stored character and needs no keypoints at all.

Motion: sprites are small, so pose bigger than life. A run or sprint leans the
upper body 10 to 15° toward the way the character faces, on every frame of the
cycle: in the image, the neck sits ahead of the midpoint of the hips (left of it
for any west-facing direction, right of it for any east-facing one). The head
moves forward with the neck but does not tip down with the body.

get_image returns exactly len(keypoints) images — the reference frame is not
echoed back. Play them in order.

Limits: sprite max 256x256; 3 to 15
frames, each skeleton holding all 18 humanoid joints.

Cost: priced by generation time, which barely moves with length, so every
legal frame count falls in one of three steps — 3 frames = 2 generations,
4 to 14 = 3, 15 = 4.
Generation time: ~3-6 minutes (async). Poll with get_image(job_id).

description.description: What the character LOOKS like, as a noun phrase: 'blonde vampire with a red cape'. Colours, clothing, held items — not the motion, which the skeletons carry.

direction.description: Facing of the sprite (south = towards the camera).

keypoints.description: The motion: one skeleton per frame you get back, 3-15 frames. Each is a list of all 18 joints, {"label": "RIGHT KNEE", "x": 0.52, "y": 0.71, "z_index": 9}, with x/y as fractions 0-1 of the image. The 18 labels, exactly (every one required once per frame, order does not matter): NOSE, NECK, RIGHT SHOULDER, RIGHT ELBOW, RIGHT ARM, LEFT SHOULDER, LEFT ELBOW, LEFT ARM, RIGHT HIP, RIGHT KNEE, RIGHT LEG, LEFT HIP, LEFT KNEE, LEFT LEG, RIGHT EYE, LEFT EYE, RIGHT EAR, LEFT EAR. That set and order are OpenPose COCO-18, so `ARM` is the WRIST and `LEG` is the ANKLE (shoulder -> elbow -> ARM, hip -> knee -> LEG) and a COCO-18 pose from an external tool maps across 1:1. LEFT/RIGHT are the character's own sides, not the viewer's: facing `east` the RIGHT limbs are the near ones, mirrored for `west`, near-equal for `south`/`north`. `z_index` is a draw order — any int, default 0; no template prescribes values for it, it is yours. `depth` is optional (0-255, ~128 = the body's centre, higher = nearer the camera); left out, it is taken from the template body for this direction — which is the easier path, since that is where near/far already comes from (a mannequin at side/east runs RIGHT ARM 156 against LEFT ARM 100).

first_frame_keypoints.description: The skeleton of the pose first_frame is already IN, same 18 joints and labels as `keypoints`. The model redraws that frame first and learns the background key and the colours from the redraw, so a skeleton that does not match the image quietly costs transparency and colour accuracy. This frame is not returned. To get these for your own sprite, call the `estimate_skeleton` tool on it, then again with the job_id it returns: it gives all 18 joints in exactly this shape and label order, x/y as fractions 0-1 of YOUR image, so they drop straight in here. Any size up to 256x256 works with no padding from you. 0.1 generations per call; a fully transparent frame is refused before anything is charged.

template_id.description: The body a joint's missing `depth` is taken from. A quadruped posed with mannequin depth comes out flat.

view.description: Camera angle the sprite is drawn at. Must match the sprite, or the motion is posed for a different camera.

no_background.description: True (default) returns the frames on transparency.

tools.name: estimate_skeleton
tools.description:
Estimate the skeleton of a humanoid sprite: its 18 joints, in exactly the
shape animate_with_skeleton_v3 takes.

Two calls: estimate_skeleton(image=...) queues it and returns a job id (usually
done in ~10-20 s, longer when the queue is busy); estimate_skeleton(job_id=...)
returns the keypoints once it is done (wait_for_jobs waits for it).

Pass the result as animate_with_skeleton_v3's `first_frame_keypoints` (the pose
the sprite is in), and use it as the starting point for each frame of
`keypoints` (the motion: move the joints frame by frame). x/y are fractions 0-1
of the image you sent; labels come in the order animate_with_skeleton_v3
lists them.

Humanoids only: the 18 joints are a person's. A fully transparent image is
refused before anything is charged.

Cost: 0.1 generations, charged when the estimate is done.

image.description: The character sprite, on a transparent background: `character:<id>:<direction>` (a rotation), `job:<id>` or `job:<id>:<index>` (an image tool result), `gallery:<id>`, `object:<id>[:<direction>]`, `upload:<id>`, a pixelart_workbench result id, an https or data URL of a PNG, or base64. One frame, up to 256x256; any size within that works (no padding needed).

job_id.description: The job id an earlier estimate_skeleton(image=...) returned: reads its keypoints once it is done. Pass image or job_id, not both.

tools.name: pixelart_workbench
tools.description:
Run one pixel-art command on a drawing or image you already made. This is
the engine's own command line: it checks work, explains it and improves it.

Commands: check and explain (read-only):
- lint <id> [--rules outline_gap,orphan_pixel,…] — pixel-art defects, each
  naming the node and command that drew them
- inspect <id> --region x0,y0,x1,y1 --scale 10 — a zoomed crop with its
  exact colours, to LOOK at: the id it returns still holds the whole
  picture, so passing it on sends the full canvas and not the region.
  `split … --count` below is what actually cuts a piece out
- measure <id> --at x,y — what is at a pixel and who drew it
- explain <id> — resolved geometry, per-command footprints, before rendering
- motion / storyboard / silhouette / reveal / clusters / parts <id> — reports
- score <id> — a 0-100 pixel-art discipline score with a breakdown
- compare <id> <id> — two results side by side
Improve (returns a NEW drawing id):
- shade <id> --band 2 --light=-1,-1 — banded shading along a colour ramp
- selout <id> — selective outlining; reoutline / clean-lines / aa / mirror
- cluster <id> --at x,y --action recolor --color <name> — one guarded cluster
- repair <id> — deterministic cleanup of drift, strays, fringe and noise
Sheets and frames (returns a NEW image id):
- split <image> --grid 3x3 [--count n] — a sprite sheet, strip or grid as an
  animation, one frame per cell (columns x rows). --count keeps the first n
  cells and drops the rest, so `split <image> --grid 2x1 --count 1` is the
  free exact crop of the left half, `--grid 1x2 --count 1` the top half, and
  a one-cell result downloads as image.png (a multi-frame one has no
  image.png, only frames.png — which is why a plain 2x1 split cannot be
  handed on as a single picture). Cells must divide the canvas evenly; the
  error names the counts that fit. Without --count, trailing cells that are
  one flat colour are dropped
- join <image> <image> … [--as sheet|rows|animation] [--columns n] — pictures
  or animations as one sprite sheet, one per row, or one animation
- scale <image> --by 4 — the same picture or animation bigger, each pixel a
  4x4 block (a sticker, a print); nothing is redrawn
A result comes back as an image in the reply AND as a no-auth URL the reply
prints, `/mcp/pixel-tools/<id>/image.png` (`frames.png` for the frames of a
multi-frame one) — so a sheet you joined is both readable inline and
downloadable. Sheets hold at most 1024 px a side; `join` refuses a larger
one rather than shrinking the art, and says how many frames do fit.
Craft operations need colour ramps: run `extract-palette <id>` first, then
pass `--ramps skin=dark,mid,light`.
Authoring: `edit <id> --changes '[…]'` applies exact pixel operations and
`draw <id> --recipe '{…}'` builds or revises a layered scene; both take JSON
whose fields are NOT listed here. Colours in that JSON are always `#RRGGBB`
or `#RRGGBBAA` with alpha `00` or `ff` — `rgb()` and bare hex are refused,
and nothing strips the `#`, since argv is a JSON list rather than a shell
line. Every `edit` change carries `operation`, `layer`, `frames` (ONE-based)
and `reason`; coordinates are zero-based and a `region` is `[x0,y0,x1,y1]`
inclusive. Then its own fields: `patch_pixels` takes `pixels`, a list of
`[x,y,expected,replacement]` (1-10000, each assigned only where the pixel
already holds `expected`, so a mismatch fails the pass); `copy_region` takes
`source_layer`, `source_frame`, `region`, `at` `[x,y]`; `map_colors` takes
`region` and `colors` `{"#from":"#to"}` (alpha must match); `flood_fill`
`seed`/`expected`/`color`; `brush` `points` plus `color`; `outline` `mode`
(outside|inside|recolor|erase). The full contracts and any command's flags
are one free call away: `describe edits | paint | outline | draw | animation
| motion | scenes | review`, `<command> -h`, `describe cli`.
Free for subscribers.

argv.description: One command line, e.g. 'lint <drawing_id> --rules outline_gap' or ['edit', '<id>', '--changes', '[…]']. Omit it for the playbook. A subject is an id or an image reference — never a file path; the server writes the output and returns a new id. A reference is `character:<id>:<direction>` for a rotation, `character:<id>:<direction>:<animation>` for every frame of that animation (the display name, type or [group: ...] id get_character prints), the same two forms for `object:<id>` (a one-direction object's direction is the literal `unknown`), `gallery:<id>`, `job:<id>`, `upload:<id>`, a data URL, an https link or base64. That is how a stored animation's pixels come back inline without downloading anything. Start with 'describe cli' for the full command list.

mode.description: low (default): act directly, fewest tokens — one decisive image per result. high: think openly — fuller evidence and a review checklist; write your plan and observations in `notes`. Use the mode the user asked for.

notes.description: What you observed and what this step should achieve, in a few sentences (high mode: always; low: optional). On the first call, include the user's request. Stored with the step to improve these tools.

tools.name: vfx_workbench
tools.description:
Make an animated pixel-art effect (spell, hit, explosion, aura, projectile,
weather...) yourself, around the user's sprite or on its own: drop in tuned
parts, write layers, look at every render, then export. Export saves it to the
user's My effects on pixellab.ai (re-editable there with sliders) and returns a
GIF and a spritesheet PNG + JSON; --game-pack adds a ZIP of every piece for a game
engine (--part <id> just one). Free for subscribers.

Commands:
- start [--sprite <image>] [--fps N] [--projectile <image>]
  [--preset <name> | --effect <effect id>] -> step id
- <step id> <tool> '<JSON>' -> add_part, set_part, remove_part, throw, render,
  get_preset, get_part, list_parts; a change returns a new step id
- <step id> export [--name N] [--replace <effect id>] [--game-pack | --part <id>]
- effects [--limit N] [--after <effect id>] -> the user's My effects (ids)
- delete <effect id> -> removes it from My effects for good
- describe start | parts | recipe | craft | cookbook | edits | presets | tools
Limits, which are this tool's own and NOT the website VFX Creator's: the
effect canvas is 16-1024 px a side in whole pixels (no multiple-of-4 rule
here), fps is 1-60 and defaults to 12, `loop` is a true/false field on the
recipe (default false; whole-number part cycle counts are what make a looping
one seamless), and frames go up to 120 under a pixel
budget of frames x width x height <= 32 x 1024 x 1024 — so 120 frames up to a
512 px canvas, 81 at 640, 56 at 768 and 32 at 1024. A `--sprite` is the
stricter one: at most 32 frames, each at most 512x512.
Sprites and exports are pixelart_workbench ids, so the two work together.
Start with describe start.

argv.description: One command, e.g. ['start', '--sprite', 'character:<id>:south'], ['<step id>', 'add_part', '{"name": "fire_burst"}'] or ['<step id>', 'export', '--name', 'Fireball']. Omit it for the guide.

mode.description: low (default): act directly, fewest tokens — one decisive image per result. high: think openly — fuller evidence and a review checklist; write your plan and observations in `notes`. Use the mode the user asked for.

notes.description: What you observed and what this step should achieve, in a few sentences (high mode: always; low: optional). On the first call, include the user's request. Stored with the step to improve these tools.

tools.name: save_to_asset
tools.description:
Save pixel art into one of your characters, objects, Creator gallery
images or tilesets, replacing a rotation, one direction of an animation, a
gallery image or a tileset's tiles — or add it to the gallery as a new image
(free, no generation).

Use it to keep a fix made with pixelart_workbench or another image tool: the
character and object creators, the Creator gallery, the map editor, downloads
and game projects then show the new pixels. The image must match what it replaces —
the same canvas size and the same number of frames; a different size can go
to the gallery as a new image. Save each direction with its own call. The
replaced frames are kept: the reply gives the save_to_asset call that puts
them back.

Examples:
- save_to_asset(image="<workbench id>", target="character:<id>:south")
- save_to_asset(image="<workbench id>", target="character:<id>:east:<group id>")
- save_to_asset(image="<workbench id>", target="object:<id>")
- save_to_asset(image="<workbench id>", target="gallery:<id>")
- save_to_asset(image="<workbench id>", target="gallery:new",
  description="knight holding a sword, idle")
- save_to_asset(image="<edited sheet>", target="tileset:<id>")

image.description: What to save: a pixelart_workbench result id (`<id>`, or `<id>:<view>` for a drawing), `job:<id>` / `job:<id>:<index>` (an image tool result), `upload:<id>` (an image POSTed to /v2/uploads), an https or data URL of a PNG or GIF, or base64. A PNG is one frame, even a strip: an animation's frames go as a GIF (one duration for all), a multi-image `job:<id>` or a multi-frame pixelart_workbench result.

target.description: Where to save it. A rotation: `character:<id>:<direction>`, `object:<id>:<direction>`, or `object:<id>` for a one-direction object. One direction of an animation: the same with `:<group id>` added (get_character / get_object show each animation's [group: …] id). A Creator gallery image: `gallery:<id>` to replace it (list_images shows each image's reference), `gallery:new` to add the image as a new one. A top-down or sidescroller tileset: `tileset:<id>` with its whole sheet (the download_png layout, same size), keeping its id and tile layout.

description.description: Only with target="gallery:new": what the image shows, kept as its gallery description so the website and list_images(search=...) can find it.

name.description: Only with target="gallery:new": the image's name, as the website's Rename sets it. Without one, a game project shows the description's first 60 characters, so give distinct names to images whose descriptions start alike.

tools.name: sandbox_create_session
tools.description: Create a sandbox session for a game project. Returns session_id + file tree + git log. Working directory: /workspace. Tools: Node.js 20, npm, git, tsc. Session expires after 30 min idle.

tools.name: list_projects
tools.description: List your projects with IDs: game projects (with branches and git clone URLs) and folders, which only group assets on the website. add_to_project files assets into either; manage_project makes, renames or deletes a folder.

kind.description: 'game' for game projects only, 'folder' for folders only, 'all' both

tools.name: sandbox_destroy_session
tools.description: Destroy a sandbox session. Syncs to storage by default.

tools.name: sandbox_bash
tools.description: Run a shell command in the sandbox (/workspace). Available: node, npm, git, tsc, and `wrangler deploy` — builds + deploys the game's unified Cloudflare Worker (frontend + /api + multiplayer /room -> {slug}.pixellab.run) and runs a smoke test. Use `wrangler deploy` to deploy (there is no separate deploy tool); `wrangler tail` shows the worker's runtime logs. Don't run build.sh / npm build directly — wrangler deploy builds.

timeout.description: Seconds before the command is killed. Default 300; a command that runs `wrangler deploy` gets at least 1200 (a build on a large asset library takes minutes).

tools.name: sandbox_run
tools.description:
Code Mode: run a JavaScript snippet in the project sandbox (Node, cwd /workspace) to do many file/shell ops in ONE call instead of chaining sandbox_read/write/edit/bash. Your code is an async function body with a typed `sandbox` API + console.log:
  sandbox.read(path)->string · sandbox.write(path,content) · sandbox.edit(path,old,new) (errors if old not found) · sandbox.ls(dir?)->string[] · sandbox.sh(cmd)->stdout
`return` a value to report it. Example: `const p=JSON.parse(sandbox.read('website/package.json')); console.log(p.name); return sandbox.ls('website/src');`  Returns console output + the returned value (or the error). Use `sandbox.sh('wrangler deploy')` to deploy.

tools.name: sandbox_read
tools.description: Read a file from the sandbox. Returns content with line numbers.

tools.name: sandbox_write
tools.description: Create or overwrite a file in the sandbox. Creates parent directories automatically.

tools.name: sandbox_edit
tools.description: Edit a file via search-and-replace. old_string must match exactly once.

tools.name: sandbox_sync
tools.description: Save current git state to persistent storage.

tools.name: sandbox_deploy_worker
tools.description: Build and deploy a Cloudflare Worker for a chat project. Deploys the unified Worker (frontend + /api + multiplayer /room) to {project_slug}.pixellab.run. Requires an active sandbox session.

tools.name: sandbox_undeploy
tools.description: Remove deployed files from S3 and invalidate CloudFront cache for a project branch. Use after deleting a project or to clean up a stale preview deployment.

tools.name: sandbox_playtest
tools.description: Playtest a deployed game using a vision AI subagent. The subagent opens the game in a browser, takes screenshots, and interacts via keyboard/mouse following your instruction. Returns a text report of observations. Takes 30-60s. Cost: ~1 generation, usually less.

tools.name: sandbox_read_image
tools.description: Read an image file from the sandbox and analyze it with a vision model. Returns a text description of the image contents. Cost: ~1 generation, usually less.

path.description: Path to the image file in the sandbox (e.g. 'game/assets/player.png').

question.description: What to analyze about the image — be specific (e.g. 'Is the player sprite facing south?', 'What colors are used in this tileset?').

tools.name: chat_list_conversations
tools.description: List your chat conversations. Excludes branches. Shows processing status.

project_id.description: Filter by project ID

tools.name: chat_get_messages
tools.description: Get messages from a conversation. Strips HTML from assistant responses.

tools.name: chat_send_message
tools.description: Send a message to a chat conversation and wait for the agent response. Creates a new conversation if conversation_id is not provided. The agent runs in background (building games, creating assets, etc). Polls until the agent finishes, then returns the assistant's reply. Typical response time: 30s-5min depending on task complexity. Cost: the agent's model usage, billed like a /chat message on the website; the reply states what the turn cost.

content.description: Message to send to the agent

conversation_id.description: Conversation ID. Omit to create a new conversation.

project_id.description: Project ID (used when creating a new conversation)

tools.name: agent_list
tools.description:
List the deployed AI agents you own (the 'deploy your own agent' projects). Returns each
agent's slug — pass it as `agent` to agent_inspect / agent_talk.

tools.name: agent_inspect
tools.description:
Debug a deployed agent's LIVE runtime: its state, recent chat, LLM/tool traces (errors first,
with the model's real input/output), and grown memory (journal/agenda/lessons/feedback). Use this
to see what the agent ACTUALLY did before changing its source. `focus='traces'` zooms in on bad turns.

agent.description: Agent slug (omit if you only have one)

tools.name: agent_talk
tools.description:
Send a message to a deployed agent (as its owner) and get its reply — to test how it responds
while you're working on it. Goes through the agent's normal chat loop (so it may run its tools).

message.description: What to say to the agent

agent.description: Agent slug (omit if you only have one)

tools.name: get_balance
tools.description: Check your account balance: remaining credits (USD) and subscription generations.

tools.name: get_upload_url
tools.description:
Get a URL to upload a local image file to, without needing your API token.

Use it whenever you have an image on disk and a tool wants an image: send
the file with one curl, and pass the `upload:<id>` it returns to any
parameter that takes an image URL (image_urls, reference_image_url,
init_image_url, a style_image "url" ...). This avoids pasting base64 into a
tool call, which clients truncate and can corrupt. Free.

The URL works for 15 minutes and for any number of files. Uploads are kept
3 days. An animated GIF keeps all its frames.

tools.name: search_knowledge
tools.description:
Search the Phaser/game dev knowledge base for tips, patterns, and code examples.

Returns semantically matched tips from the curated knowledge base — useful
for Phaser 4 patterns, TypeScript game dev, Vite build issues, map systems,
collision, camera follow, and other game builder topics.

query.description: Search query — describe the Phaser/TypeScript/game dev topic you need help with (e.g. 'camera follow player', 'collision detection', 'map transitions').

tools.name: cancel_job
tools.description:
Cancel a pending or processing background job.

Releases the concurrency slot immediately so you can start new work.
Already-completed or already-failed jobs are left unchanged.

Cost: work that has not started costs nothing to cancel, but a job already
generating is billed for the work done — an image request already sent
usually costs its full price — and an earlier batch of an animation stays
billed. Without "generation stopped" in the reply, work running in another
process may still finish and charge; get_image on the job then names the
saved result. A job that fails on its own is never charged, and one that
completed cannot be cancelled: its charge stands.

tools.name: wait_for_jobs
tools.description:
Wait for your running generations instead of sleeping and polling.

Returns as soon as min_finished (default 1) of your pending/processing jobs
finish, immediately when none are running, or at the timeout. Free. Then call
the matching get_* tool for the result; call wait_for_jobs again for the jobs
still running. It watches every job on the account, so it also lists ones the
user started on the website or with another client.

timeout_seconds.description: Give up waiting after this many seconds (jobs keep running). If your client times out the call itself (some stop a tool at ~60s), pass a value under that limit and call again.

min_finished.description: Return once this many of your running jobs have finished (or all of them, if fewer are running). 1 frees you to fill a slot the moment one opens; raise it for a large batch so one call covers several.
